At room temperature, pure C3S only exists in the T1 form, and various impurities have to be introduced into C3S to obtain the other higher temperature forms [1–3]. Extensive efforts have been made to study the polymorphic structure of C3S in past decades. However, due to the complicated structure and the difficulty in preparing single crystals of C3S, the analysis of the crystal structure of C3S has been mainly based on powder X-ray diffraction (XRD), differential thermal analysis (DTA) and optical microscopy [1–3]. Consequently, the atomic structure of different C3S polymorphs and the relations between the polymorphs have not been fully understood. Only three polymorphs (R, M3, and T1) have been solved by X-ray single-crystal methods [4–9]. The measured structures are similar with respect to the positions of the Ca2+ and O2− ions and the Si atoms but differ markedly in the orientations of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra, which show varying degrees of disorder [3,10]. The orientational disorder of the tetrahedra that characterize the M3 superstructure has features intermediate between those of R and T1 [8,10]. In addition, the mean coordination number of Ca2+ ions in M3 is also between those of R and T1 [8,10]. All C3S polymorphs, except T3 and R, have been confirmed to possess structural modulations [2,7,8,11–16]. The structural modulations of T1, M1, M2 and M3 C3S were systematically investigated by Urabe et al. using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) [11,12]. The superstructure of T1 was found to include both distortion of the silicate tetrahedra in their orientations and periodic deviation of cations from their average positions [11]. The monoclinic superstructures are believed to be caused by the periodic ordering of the orientations of the apices of the silicate tetrahedral [5,6,8,12]. With the development of Rietveld analysis and power diffraction, various structural models for T2, T3, M1 and M3 polymorphs have been developed based on the atomic models determined by the previous single-crystal experiments [14–20]. It has been shown that the structural differences between the polymorphs include slight shifts of the atomic positions and changes in the orientational order or disorder of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra associated with consequent changes in the coordination of calcium ions [2–20].
Infrared (IR) spectroscopy can be used to identify structures because molecules and functional groups absorb specific frequencies that are characteristic of their structure. The application of IR spectroscopy in the field of cement chemistry dates back to the 5th international symposium on the chemistry of cement, Tokyo (1968). As a simple, quick, and inexpensive analytical technique, IR spectroscopy can provide ample information on the structure of minerals and has been widely used to study cement and hydration products [21–33]. The IR spectra of pure C3S and its ion-stabilized forms have been studied [21–27]. However, changes in the IR spectra of C3S solid solutions were mainly attributed to the effect of substituent ions, and little attention has been given to the influence of variation in polymorphs.
Like C3S, dicalcium silicate (C2S) has a nesosilicate type structure with isolated [SiO4]4− tetrahedra, and the different C2S polymorphs mainly differ in the orientations of their [SiO4]4− tetrahedra. The vibration frequencies of C2S vary considerably depending on polymorphs [34]. Therefore, it is reasonable to hypothesize that variations in the polymorphs of C3S contribute to the differences in the IR spectra of C3S as well. Our recent research has shown that the IR spectra of C3S solid solutions (M3 form) with different compositions are similar but are quite different from that of T1 C3S [35]. However, there are few studies focused on the IR spectra of different C3S polymorphs due to the complexity of the C3S structure. The relations between foreign ions, the polymorphic structure and the IR spectra of C3S are not fully understood.
The main objective of this work is to obtain IR spectra of different C3S polymorphs and to understand the polymorphic structure of C3S. The effects of variation in the polymorphs and the introduction of substituent ions on the IR spectra of C3S were discerned by synthesizing samples with differing types and amounts of foreign ions but the same polymorphic form. The results from this study will help to further understand the polymorphic structure of C3S and to promote better use of IR spectroscopy in the study of cement and hydration products.
2_Material and methods:
2.1 Preparation of specimens C3S and its solid solutions were synthesized by a conventional ceramic method. Analytical grade chemical reagents CaCO3, SiO2, Na2CO3·10H2O, K2CO3, MgO, Al2O3, Fe2O3, BaO, CaHPO4·2H2O and CaSO4·2H2O were used as the starting materials. Table 1  shows the nominal dosages, expressed as oxide, used to prepare different polymorphs of C3S solid solutions. SiO2 was first calcined at 950°C to eliminate the volatile constituents and was then ground in an agate mortar for 1h to promote the formation of C3S. Second, a mixture of 3mol CaCO3 and 1mol SiO2 with different types and amounts of impurities was homogenized for 5h in a homemade mixer (prepared pure C3S was used as the starting material for single-ion doping). The mixtures were ground again in an agate mortar for 0.5h and then pressed into cylindrical pellets. The pellets were calcined at 1600°C for 6h and rapidly cooled with a flow of air. The samples were reground, pelletized and heated until a constant free lime (f-CaO) content was reached (less than 0.2%, mass weight, the same as below).
2.2 Testing method The free lime contents were determined by the ethylene glycol method. All powder diffraction data were recorded with a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffraction diffractometer in the range of 5–65° (2θ) with a step size of 0.01° using CuKα1,2 and a 1D position sensitive detector (PSD) (Lynxeye) at 38kV and 270mA. The Rietveld analyses of X-ray data were done using the Topas3 program. The Pearson VII function was used to fit the profile. The final globally optimized parameters were: zero shift, background, scaling factor, absorption correction, Pearson VII coefficients, lattice parameters and preferred orientation when appropriate. The atomic positions were not refined. FT-IR spectra of the samples were measured in the region 400–4000cm−1 using a Bruker TENSOR 27 Fourier transform infrared spectrometer. Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns were recorded using a TEM instrument (Model JEM-2010UHR, JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) at an accelerating voltage of 200kV.
3_Results and discussion:
3.1 Analysis of C3S polymorphs All specimens were identified as C3S. The XRD peaks of C3S between 31.5° and 33° and between 51° and 52.5° are good indicators of the symmetries of the polymorphs [3,12,13]. Fig. 1  shows selected angular ranges of the XRD patterns (CuKα2 stripped) for the C3S samples. The differences between samples are evident. In the XRD pattern of R C3S, there are two characteristic peaks between 31.5° and 33°, and one between 51° and 52.5°, corresponding to the 009,   2 −  04  and 220 reflections, respectively. The   2 −  04  and 220 reflections split with a decrease in crystal symmetry of C3S. Pure C3S (Sample X1) is triclinic, T1, as expected, and both the   2 −  04  and 220 reflections are split into triplet peaks, presenting four reflections between 31.5° and 33° and three between 51° and 52.5°. The XRD pattern of T2 C3S is similar to that of T1 C3S. The main difference is that the central doublet peaks between 31.5° and 33° are closer for T2 C3S [12] and show a tendency to merge into a single peak. In the T3 powder pattern, there are only three peaks between 31.5° and 33°, and the last two peaks between 51° to 52.5° have a tendency to merge. In the monoclinic polymorph, the   2 −  04  and 220 reflections only split into doublets. Sample X4 presents phase coexistence. The main phase can be identified as M1 C3S [12]. Sample X5 presents an M3-type powder pattern [16]. Based on the X-ray diffraction data, quantitative analysis of C3S polymorph was performed using the Rietveld method. The T1 and T2 structures were fitted to that of Golovastikov et al. (triclinic C3S) [5]. T3 was fitted to the T3 structural model provided by De la Torre et al. [16]. M1 was fitted to the average monoclinic model provided by de Noirfontaine et al. [18]. The M3 and R structures were fitted to that of Nishi et al. (monoclinic) [8] and Jeffery (rhombohedral) [4], respectively. In Fig. 2 , the measured and calculated X-ray diffractions of different samples are shown together with the difference plots. The insets feature the fingerprint regions which are unique to different polymorphs. Table 2  gives the Rietveld quantitative phase analysis results of the C3S polymorph. It can be seen from Fig. 2 and Table 2 that the five samples (X1, X2, X3, X5 and X6) fit well with the corresponding structural model. However, two crystal structures are required to fit the XRD pattern of sample X4. Although the T1 structure of Golovastikov can be used for T3 C3S, the combined use of the T3 and M1 structure model resulted in better fits than the mixed use of T1 and M1, indicating that the quantification of C3S polymorphs is strongly affected by the choice of the structural model. TEM further confirmed that the main phase present in X4 is M1 C3S. Based on the pseudohexagonal subcell (a=7.062Å, b=7.063Å, c=25.026Å, α=89.89°, β=90.41°, γ=119.59°), a typical SAED pattern for M1 with a one-dimensional incommensurate structure was identified (shown in Fig. 3 ). It can be expressed as a linear combination of reciprocal vectors ±m/5.4 (2a H ∗ +5c H ∗), where m=±1 or ±2, in accordance with the data given by Urabe et al. [12] and Min et al. [36]. All polymorphs can be regarded as minute deformations of the rhombohedral structure [11–13]. The lattice parameters of the pseudohexagonal or hexagonal average structures (based on the R polymorph) for different polymorphs were refined by the least-squares method and are given in Table 3 . The lattice parameters of the M3 subcell are smaller than those of the other polymorphs, especially the parameter c and the cell volume. De la Torre et al. found that the unit cell volumes of M3 alite decrease with increasing amount of MgO by comparing the works of Mumme [9] and Nishi [8]. However, the MgO content of X5 is the same as sample X6, indicating that the shrinkage was probably related to the structure of the M3 polymorph rather than its composition. M3 C3S synthesized with different compositions also gave similar results. Viani et al. also found that there is a clear change in the lattice parameters and the thermal expansion coefficients of the monoclinic C3S solid solution (Ca2.879Mg0.112Al0.0439Si0.971O5) at approximately 900°C, which is due to the phase change between two monoclinic forms [37]. Thus, changes in the lattice parameters of M3 C3S are probably related to the variations in the polymorph. The differences in the deformation of the subcells of monoclinic C3S were attributed to differences in the ordering of the orientations of the apices of the silicate tetrahedra occurring along special directions (directions of the modulation waves) [12]. According to the literatures [4,7], silicon ions are on the c axis, approximately two of the three tetrahedra point down the c axis, and the others point up the cH axis in R C3S. However, there are additional ill-defined G–gauche–orientations in M3 C3S [8]. Thus, the shrinkage of the M3 subcell might correlate with unique changes in the arrangement of [SiO4]4− along the cH axis. More IR evidence will be discussed in the following sections.
3.2 IR spectra of different C3S polymorphs The infrared absorption bands of C3S in the region 400–4000cm−1 are mainly from the vibration of [SiO4]4− groups. Isolated [SiO4]4− tetrahedra have four vibration modes, including symmetric stretching vibration (ν1), asymmetric stretching (ν3), in-plane bending vibration (ν2) and out-of-plane bending (ν4). Ideally, the four Si-O sp3 hybrid orbits in a [SiO4]4− tetrahedron are completely equivalent with the same number of electrons on each track. These electrons repel each other and keep as far away as possible; thus, [SiO4]4− can maintain a regular tetrahedron symmetry when free of outside interference. Theoretically, the symmetric stretching ν1 of an ideal [SiO4]4− tetrahedron is not active for IR. The IR spectra of different C3S polymorphs are given in Fig. 4 , which shows that there is a decrease in the band splitting with increasing structural symmetry of C3S. The vibration bands for different C3S polymorphs are listed in Table 4 . The main vibrations of pure C3S (T1 form) are: symmetric stretching of the silicate tetrahedra [SiO4]4− (ν3) at 996, 938, 906 and 883cm−1; symmetric stretching (ν1) at 846, 834 and 812cm−1; out-of-plane bending vibration (ν4) at 525cm−1; and in-plane bending vibration (ν2) centred at approximately 464 and 455cm−1. These assignments are in accordance with the data given in previous studies [22–26]. The IR spectrum of T2 C3S is quite similar to that of T1 C3S. Both T1 and T2 C3S show forbidden bands corresponding to symmetric vibrations, indicating that the distortion from an ideal tetrahedron structure is caused by [SiO4]4−. This is supported by the finding of Peterson [14], who determined the structure of pure C3S with the T2 polymorph using in situ, high-temperature synchrotron powder diffraction combined with Rietveld refinement and showed that the SiO4 tetrahedra of T2 C3S were highly distorted and the OSiO bond angles showed significant deviation from the tetrahedral angle. Since the charge of the oxygen ion in [SiO4]4− was balanced by Ca2+ ions, the distortion of [SiO4]4− is probably due to the effect of the asymmetrical Ca2+ ion force field resulting from the poor structural symmetry of the T1 and T2 polymorphs. It is supported by the finding of Urabe et al., who found that cations periodically deviated from their average positions in T1 C3S [11]. Although T3 C3S belongs to the same triclinic system as T1 and T2, there are significant changes in the IR spectrum of T3. It has a smaller number of bands than the previous spectra. The symmetric stretching bands disappear, the most striking feature of which is that the sharp peak at approximately 812cm−1 vanishes, indicating that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra in T3 C3S retain a regular tetrahedron symmetry. This result is in agreement with the structural descriptions for T3 C3S given by De la Torre and Peterson [16,19]. Therefore, there are larger differences in the structure between T3 and T2 C3S than between T2 and T1 C3S. This conclusion is in agreement with the relatively large transformation enthalpy for the T2–T3 transition [2,13]. The T1–T2 transition has an extremely small transformation enthalpy and can be detected by microscopy, while the T2–T3 transition has a large transformation enthalpy and is invisible to light microscopy [38]. The collapse of the superstructure was first proposed by Bigare et al. [13] to explain the large peak in the DTA curve for the T2–T3 transition. This explanation was further supported by Peterson, who observed the existence of the superstructure in T1 and T2 for pure C3S using in situ, high-temperature synchrotron powder diffraction [14]. Regourd also suggested that the transition, which has no influence on the “megascopic” optical properties, might be attributed to the formation of the superstructure due to the orientation disorder of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra and changes in the Ca coordination [39]. Based on the above results from the IR spectra of T1, T2 and T3 C3S, this phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that the position of the Ca2+ and O2− ions and the Si atoms probably does not change, nor does the atomic packing density; consequently, there is no change in the refractive index. The large transformation enthalpy for the T2–T3 transition is mainly caused by changes in the deformation and orientation disorder of [SiO4]4− tetrahedra in the T2–T3 transition due to the displacement of the O atoms of [SiO4]4− tetrahedra, which also causes subsequent changes in the coordination of the surrounding Ca2+ ions. Despite the fact that there are major changes in the IR spectrum of T3 compared with that of T1 and T2, the IR spectra of the other three higher symmetry (temperature) polymorphs, M1, M3 and R C3S, are similar to that of T3, and only small shifts of the in-plane bending (ν2) to higher wave numbers were observed. The absence of the symmetric stretching bands shows that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra in M1, M3 and R have an approximately regular tetrahedron symmetry. Special shifts of the asymmetric stretching bands (ν3) at approximately 938cm−1 and 884cm−1 to 925cm−1 and 890cm−1, respectively, were observed for M3 C3S, which indicates that the chemical environment of [SiO4]4− in M3 C3S is different from that in the other polymorphs. It corresponds with the analytical results of XRD and can be explained by the changes in the arrangement of [SiO4]4− along the cH axis. With the increase in the crystal symmetry of C3S, the number of bands for the polymorphs T1→T2→T3→M1→M3→R decreases, and the peaks are broadened. The symmetric stretching bands with a sharp peak approximately 812cm−1 disappear in the spectra of T3, M1, M3 and R C3S, indicating that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra retain a regular tetrahedron symmetry in their structures. The structure of M3 C3S is slightly different from that of the other polymorphs with respect to the orientation of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra along the cH axis. The monoclinic superstructures are caused by periodical ordering of the orientations of the apices of the silicate tetrahedral [12]. Thus, the transitions between R, M3, M2 and M1 mainly involve changes in the orientation of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra. However, the differences in the superstructures of the average monoclinic and triclinic unit cells consist of both small displacements of calcium atoms and changes in the orientational order or disorder of the SiO4 tetrahedra [2]. The T3–T2 transition involves both local tetrahedral distortion of [SiO4]4− and changes in their orientation of. In T1 C3S, periodic deviations of cations from their average positions occurs, in addition to the distortion of silicate tetrahedral [11]. The relationship between C3S polymorphs remains unclear. To understand the atomic structure of the polymorphs and their relations, more work has to be done.
3.3 The effect of foreign ions on the IR spectra of C3S T1, T3 and M3 C3S with various types and amounts of foreign ions were systematically synthesized (see Table 5 ). Special attention is given to the amount of both Al2O3 and Fe2O3, which are amphoteric in nature and are usually considered top provide the best evidence to assess the effect of foreign ions on the IR spectra of C3S. Fig. 5  shows the IR spectra of T1, T3 and M3 C3S. The IR spectra of the C3S samples with different compositions but the same polymorphic form are almost identical. There are no changes in the peak position or number of peaks in the IR spectra of T1 C3S with single doping of either Al2O3 or Fe2O3 (see Fig. 5a). The IR spectra of T3 C3S with single doping of Al2O3 or Fe2O3 and with combined doping of multiple ions are shown in Fig. 5b. No changes are observed in the IR spectra of T3 C3S with different compositions. Similarly, no effect of Al3+ on the IR spectra of M3 C3S is observed (see Fig. 5c). However, Fe3+ has been shown to have a slight effect on the IR spectrum of M3 C3S. With increasing amount of Fe3+, slight shifts of the symmetric stretching bands (ν3) to lower waver number are observed for M3 C3S (Fig. 5c). However, the most intense peak is still centred at lower wave numbers of approximately 924–932cm−1, as described above. Thus, changes in the IR spectra of C3S solid solutions mainly result from changes in the polymorphic structures. The introduction of substituent ions has a weak effect on the IR spectra of C3S. Consequently, IR spectroscopy can be used to identify the polymorphs of C3S.
4_Conclusion: The following conclusions may be drawn from the present study.  1. The IR spectrum of C3S mainly depends on the polymorph or the mixture of polymorphs present. With increasing crystal symmetry of C3S, the number of absorption bands for the polymorphs T1→T2→T3→M1→M3→R decreases, and the peaks are broadened. The effect of substituent ions in C3S on the IR characteristics is weak. FTIR spectroscopy can be used to help identify the polymorphs of C3S.   2. The IR spectrum of T2 C3S is similar to that of T1 C3S. Both show forbidden bands corresponding to symmetric vibrations, indicating that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra are strongly distorted from an ideal tetrahedron.   3. Although T3 C3S belongs to the same triclinic system as T1 and T2, significant changes in the spectrum of T3 C3S are observed, indicating greater differences in the orientations and tetrahedral configurations of [SiO4]4− in T3 C3S than in T1 and T2 C3S. It explains why the T2–T3 transition has the largest transformation enthalpy but is invisible to microscopy methods.   4. The symmetric stretching bands with a sharp peak at approximately 812cm−1 are absent in the spectra of T3, M1, M3 and R C3S, indicating that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra retain an approximately regular tetrahedron symmetry in their structures. The structure of M3 C3S is slightly different from that of the other polymorphs with respect to the orientation of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra along the cH axis.

Title: Laboratory synthesis of C3S on the kilogram scale
Abstract: An optimized process using amorphous silica for efficient C3S synthesis in the laboratory is reported: an estimated production capacity of ~2 kg C3S within a week is possible. Amorphous silica (fumed silica) was used as raw material and inter-ground with CaCO3 and water for C3S synthesis, the dried raw mixture has sufficient green strength to be self-supporting, which allows large cylinders to be placed in Platinum crucibles. The mineral composition of the sintered sample was quantified with X-ray powder diffraction using Rietveld analysis. C3S with <0.4 wt% of free CaO was sintered at a shortened residence time (≤5 h) when temperatures ≥1550 °C. The efficiency of the C3S synthesis was dramatically enhanced because of 1) increased burnability of the raw mix due to amorphous silica and very fine CaCO3 particles after grinding, 2) simplified sample preparation process avoiding pressing discs and 3) improved capacities of the crucible and furnace.
1_Introduction:
C3S (tricalcium silicate) is the major phase in Portland cement, as such many studies have been focused on the reaction of this phase alone. However, more extensive work is hindered by the difficulty in obtaining high quality C3S. It is important to realise that C3S, like Portland cement will tend to age, due to humidity in the atmosphere, if stored for too long. The best quality materials can be obtained if it is synthesized fresh for each study. Furthermore, local synthesis allows adjustment of the minor elements to obtain alite with grain growth similar to alite in Portland cement, which can then be ground to have a particle size distribution resembling Portland cement. However, most of the standard methods for preparing C3S are very time-consuming.
The methods typically reported for C3S synthesis are: solid reaction [1–14] (summarized in Table 1 ), sol-gel method [15–17]. Pechini or modified Pechini process [18] and the so-called organic steric entrapment method [19,20] were also used to synthesize C3S. For massive synthesis, the solid reaction using calcium carbonate and SiO2 (quartz or silica) is more practical and widely used. The procedures, as well as the main limitations for C3S synthesis are summarized in Table 2 . The main factors hindering the C3S synthesis are: 1) disc pressing is time-consuming; 2) long sintering time is required (>10 h); 3) capacity of Pt crucibles and furnaces are limited.
Here we report the straightforward synthesis of kilogram quantities of C3S which adapts the solid reaction method [1,21] and can be used in any laboratory equipped with a high-temperature furnace. The solid reaction routine was modified by changing the raw materials and procedures to maximize the furnace efficiency and decrease the workload of the procedures. The sintering parameters were optimized to maximize the amount of C3S which could be produced within working hours.
2_Materials and equipment/tools:
2.1 Materials and mix design Calcium carbonate (VWR) and SiO2 (silica fumed, Sigma-Aldrich) were used as raw materials for C3S synthesis. The characteristics of the raw materials and the C3S raw mix are shown in Table 3 . The source for SiO2 was amorphous fumed silicas (see Fig. 1 ) with a nominal diameter of 0.007 μm and 0.2–0.3 μm indicated by the supplier. These two fumed silicas with different particle size distribution (PSD) were used to check the feasibility to produce C3S using coarser silica (0.2 μm) instead of using 0.007 μm fumed silica for nano safety reasons. After grinding, both raw mixes made with 0.007 μm and 0.2–0.3 μm fumed silica have similar PSD (see Table 3). A correction of the mix design was needed based on actual mineral composition detected by X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) or the actual chemical composition by X-ray fluorescence (XRF) of the trial mix design. The reason for the deviation in chemical composition was moisture/solvent residue in fumed silicas so there was less SiO2 than expected in the weighed quantity. Extra amount silica will be needed to react with the excess f-CaO to compensate for this effect. The excess 3.7 wt% of CaO (by mass 476.67 g × 0.037 = 17.80 g) was compensated by 6.44 g of silica in the mix to form C3S, resulting 133.11 g of silica.
2.2 Equipment and tools The required equipment/tools are (see Fig. 2 ):  • ball milling jar up to 3 L   • milling balls (ZrO2) with diameter ~30 mm   • rolling machine to grind by rotating the ball milling jar   • cylinder moulds 1   1 Depend on the size of the platinum crucible and the inside height of the furnace, in this paper the ASTM moulds with the dimension of φ70mm × 140 mm for mortar test was used     • ladles, filters and containers (i.e. salad spinner) to separate the ball and mixed raw materials   • high-temperature furnace (up to at least 1600 °C)   •  Pt crucible   • strengthened crucible tongs with extra-long handle and a fire proof base   • fan for cooling process (cleaned compressed air can be used as well)   • a full set of protection such as heat resistance gloves, welding glasses and heat resistant helmet
2.3 Testing methods The details of the analytical techniques used: X-ray powder diffraction; Rietveld analysis, particle size distribution and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) are given in the annex.
3_Method (video can be found in Suppleme:
3.1 Preparation of C3S raw mix The raw materials were weighed according to the steps stated previously in the materials section (Section 2.1) as shown in Table 4. A summarized schematic plot of the procedures is shown in Fig. 3. Figs. 4 and 5 shows the pictures for the casting of the raw cylinder, the sintering and the quenching of the samples. More detailed steps for sample preparation are:  • Step 1:  ◦ Add grinding balls (2.4 kg of ~5 cm ZrO2 ball) into the cleaned jar (volume up to 3 L);   ◦ Weigh exact amount of SiO2 into the jar; then add CaCO3 and other oxides (i.e. Al2O3, MgO and Fe2O3 for alite synthesis) when necessary (see Table 4);   ◦ Add ~1.5 kg (mass ratio of water/materials ~2.0) of distilled water      • Step 2 2   2 Here we provide an example way of grinding. Any other grinding method (i.e. planetary ball mill) which can reduce the PSD of the raw materials can be used. :  ◦ Close the jar before putting it on a rolling machine for 24 h for a homogeneous mixing; remove any material stuck on the lid into the jar by interrupting the milling 2–3 times;      • Step 3:  ◦ Filter the paste using salad spinner by manually shaking interior colander   ◦ Transfer the paste into cylinder moulds (φ70mm × 140 mm);      • Step 4:  ◦ Dry the blends at 105 °C until constant weight (~48 h, maybe longer), make sure the cylinders are completely dried, as the moisture residue in the raw cylinders would cause damage to the furnace;      • Step 5:  ◦ Place the dried cylinder into the clean Pt crucible carefully;      • Step 6:  ◦ Carefully transport the sample together with the Pt crucible into the furnace, make sure there is enough space between the crucibles to take them out of the furnace (see Fig. 4);   ◦ After required sintering time, handle the sample with full set of high-temperature protection, quench the sintered C3S using forced air (see Fig. 5).
3.2 Sintering The sintering temperature of 1450, 1500, 1550 and 1600 °C was used coupled with residence times of 2.5, 5, 10, 15 and 20 h, respectively. A summary of the parameters is shown in Table 5. After sintering, C3S was cooled down in the forced air with a fan.
4_Safety:
4.1 Furnace and high-temperature safety      Make sure the cylinders are completely dry before putting them into the furnace, otherwise any moisture in the samples risks damaging the heating units and refractory materials inside the furnace. Make sure the green cylinder was standing still in the Pt crucible without any following pieces out of the crucible, open the furnace to check the status of the reacting cylinders once or twice, especially for the first few sintering experiments. Wear welding glasses, heat resistance helmet/head mask, chest protection, lab coat, safety shoes and heat resistance gloves when handling samples at high temperature. Special care must be taken to avoid touching the heating units when taking the sample in and out, which are extremely fragile.
4.2 Handling fumed silica The potential danger of fumed silica is inhalation hazardous, skin and/or eye contact according to OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration) [22]. In inhalation studies, none of the examined synthetic amorphous silica led to durable changes in the lung or to progressive damage comparable to silicosis [23,24]. However, when exposed to high concentration (3 mg/m3), there could be a danger to life or health according to NIOSH (The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health) [25]. The important steps for the protection are: wear N95 mask (FFP3 mask when nano powders are involved), safety glasses, hygienic cap, lab coat, gloves, and handle the fumed silica in the ventilation hood. The waste powder should be cleaned with a piece of wet cloth or paper. Fumed silica (amorphous) with larger particle size (>100 nm, i.e. 0.2 μm) was recommended to avoid handling nano particles. Constituent particles in the size range 1–100 nm was considered nano particles [26]. As long as SiO2 powder was mixed with water, there is no more danger. Principally, the rules for handling nano-particles must be followed according to the specific protocols from the institution/laboratory if nano fumed silica is used, for more details the reader is referred to the paper by Groso et al. [27].
5_Results:
The characteristic ranges of the XRD pattern accompanied by the Rietveld fitting (as shown in Fig. 6 ) showed the presence of T1 polymorph for C3S [28–30].
5.1 Optimal sintering condition The quantitative Rietveld results from the different sintering temperatures and residence times (shown in Table 5) were compiled into contour plots of the C3S and f-CaO (free lime) content as shown in Fig. 7 . These can be used to determine conditions for practical sintering [31–33]. For instance, a sample with ~96 wt% C3S and ~0.3 wt% f-CaO can be sintered at point P1, P2 or P3 as shown in Fig. 7. So, the sintering can be done with a short resistance time (≤5 h) for temperatures ≥1550 °C or a longer time (≥10 h) for temperatures ≤1500 °C. The practical choice of the sintering temperature depends on the length of the working day and the model of the furnace available. Near identical results were obtained for both the silicas used (see Table 5). Samples from different places of the cylinder were taken to check the homogeneity of the sintered C3S (as shown in Table 5). There was no significant difference in the mineral composition for samples taken from different positions. Micrographs of the raw mix and the sintered C3S (Fig. 8  (a) and (b)) also show good homogeneity. For most of the study, a heating speed of 5° per minute was used, but a faster heating speed of 7 °C/min had no negative impact on the quality of the C3S (see Table 5). This faster heating speed decreases the total synthesis time to 6.7 h which can be fitted into a normal working day when C3S is sintered at 1600 °C for 3 h (point P3 in Fig. 7). This avoids using the furnace overnight. For most of high-temperature furnaces (up to 1600–1700 °C), a heating speed of 7 °C /min is practical, as 5–10 °C/min is usually recommended.
6_Discussion and conclusion:
Here, a simplified process for C3S synthesis is reported, using amorphous silica and avoiding pressing raw mix into discs. This greatly increases the efficiency of C3S synthesis at the laboratory scale. The sintering can be done at short resistance times (≤5 h) when temperatures ≥1550 °C are used.
A detailed comparison of the protocols used for C3S synthesis is summarized in Table 6 .
The capacity of the C3S synthesis under these conditions was ~2 kg/week which was 5–10 times more than that from the traditional routine (see Table 6). The quality of the final C3S was good (with 96–98 wt% of C3S and f-CaO <0.4 wt%).
The dried cast cylinder is porous which promotes the escape of CO2 inside of the cylinder during the decomposition of the CaCO3. The resulting C3S blocks were also porous (see Fig. 8 (b)) and easy to grind.
The main aspects of improvement are (see Table 2 and Fig. 3):  •  Raw mix preparation: use cast cylinders instead of pressed discs.    •  Sintering time: improved burnability as the use of amorphous silica and decreased PSD for calcium carbonate by grinding    •  Capacity of the crucible and furnace: increased capacity as the use of cast cylinders.
The Dv50 of the calcite was decreased from 16 μm to ~4 μm after grinding (see Table 3). The simplified process by casting the paste into cylinder contributed to the capacity of the C3S synthesis.
Alite doped with oxides (i.e. Fe2O3, Al2O3, ZnO, MgO etc.) could also be produced using the procedure reported here. The homogeneity of the alite doped with chemicals with high dissolution rates in water (i.e. alkali, gypsum etc.) must be checked before moving to the massive synthesis. This is also the case when using colloidal silica (i.e. Ludox® GRACE, Sigma-Aldrich) as the source of SiO2, as colloidal silica typically contains relative high sodium content. Because the water migration and evaporation during the drying process of the raw mix might cause some inhomogeneity of these samples. The process reported here for alite synthesis could be used for belite at a lowered sintering temperature, typically at 1350 °C.

Title: Effect of ionic doping on the structure and reactivity of Portland cement tricalcium silicate
Abstract: Doping during Portland cement clinker synthesis significantly influences the stabilization and reactivity of tricalcium silicate (C3S) polymorphs. Therefore, this study investigates the effect of MgO, ZnO, and TiO2 doping (at 0.5 and 1.0 wt%) on the structural and hydration behavior of C3S. Synthesis was performed at 1500 °C for six hours, followed by characterization using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area analysis, and isothermal calorimetry. To further assess the catalytic effects of dopant ions on C3S hydration, higher doping levels (4.0 and 8.0 wt%) were also evaluated. The results show that doping promotes stabilization of the T3, M1, and M3 C3S polymorphs. Among the dopants, MgO-enhanced phases exhibited higher intrinsic reactivity. However, despite this increased reactivity, hydration rates were reduced across all systems due to a dual effect: catalytic interactions with the hydration products and the formation of a physical barrier by excess dopant. These findings provide new insights into the design of doped clinker systems for tailored hydration performance.
1_Introduction:
Doping, the deliberate incorporation of minor quantities of foreign elements or oxides to tailor material properties, is a well-established strategy in diverse industrial sectors, including semiconductor manufacturing and metallic alloy production [1,2].
Recent shifts toward alternative raw materials and alternative fuels in cement manufacture driven by environmental and economic considerations have increased the introduction of minor constituents and trace elements into the kiln system [3–5]. These unavoidable impurities, whether intentionally added or introduced through feedstocks, can significantly affect clinker mineralogy, reactivity, and performance, underscoring the importance of understanding the mechanisms and implications of doping in modern clinker production [2–7].
In the production of tricalcium silicate (C3S), the main phase of Portland cement clinker, the doping technique stabilizes one or more polymorphs at room temperature. In order to use this technique, the type of dopant ion, its content, and the synthesis temperature must be determined. These factors regulate its efficiency [8–14].
To understand the effect of doping on C3S formation, the types of solid solutions formed through this approach must first be considered. These are generally classified as interstitial or substitutional. For interstitial solid solutions, it is essential to assess whether the impurity can be accommodated within existing lattice vacancies at the synthesis temperature or if the interstitial sites are comparable in size to the dopant. In the case of substitutional solid solutions, the physicochemical properties of the dopant must be compatible with those of the host ion to be replaced. Key factors include valence, electronegativity, crystal structure, and unit cell volume [15,16].
The formation of C3S initially involves a solid substitution solution, and as the dopant ion increases, minor defects occur in the lattice, transforming it into an interstitial solution [17,18].
The C3S formed from a substitutional solid solution occurs preferentially with the substitution of the calcium ion from the dopant ion due to the type and length of the chemical bond in comparison to the silicon ion. In the crystal structure of C3S, oxygen (Oc) is bonded to silicon (covalent bond), forming the silicon tetrahedron, with a bond distance ranging from 1.64 to 1.67 Å. In contrast, calcium is bonded (ionic bond) to oxygen (Oi) with a bond distance ranging from 2.33 to 2.48 Å, making it weaker and more susceptible to substitution [19]. Studies show that dopant ions replace calcium ions due to the formation energy required to break the CaO and SiO chemical bonds [20,21].
The interstitial solid solution is more difficult to form due to the energy required to create several vacancies equivalent to the size of the impurity in the crystal structure [20,22].
Dopants can be introduced in various forms, including ions (e.g., Mg2+, Cr3+, Al3+, and Fe2+), oxides (e.g., Cr2O3, ZnO, CuO, NiO, Pb3O4, Al2O3, MgO, P2O5, Mn2O3, SO3, and BaO), or sulfates (e.g., SO4 2−, CaSO4, K₂SO4, and Na₂SO4. Among these, MgO, ZnO, and Al2O3 are the most used dopants. However, a clear correlation between dopant type and the stabilization of a specific polymorph remains elusive. This is largely due to conflicting findings reported in the literature, where the same dopant depending on its concentration can stabilize different polymorphs. Table 1  presents data from the literature on this behavior.
Despite the extensive research on doping in Portland cement clinker synthesis, a clear and consistent relationship between specific dopants and the stabilization of tricalcium silicate (C3S) polymorphs remains elusive. This uncertainty stems from the variability in experimental conditions reported across the literature, including differences in dopant concentrations, synthesis protocols, and thermal treatment parameters. As a result, it is common to find conflicting data where the same dopant stabilizes different polymorphs depending on its concentration and the synthesis route employed.
An example involves ZnO as a dopant. Urabe et al. [11] investigated ZnO additions ranging from 0.8 to 8.0 wt% under a sintering regime of 1500 °C for six hours. The authors reported that 8.0 wt% ZnO stabilized the rhombohedral (R) polymorph, while intermediate concentrations (3.2–6.4 wt%) induced transitions among triclinic (T1, T2) and monoclinic (M1, M3) forms. In contrast, Lv et al. [31] applied lower ZnO contents (0.1–3.0 wt%) at a reduced sintering temperature (1450 °C for two hours, repeated over three cycles) and observed stabilization of the M1 polymorph at lower ZnO contents, with a transition toward the R polymorph at 3.0 wt%. Similarly, Lü et al. [23], using the same conditions as Lv et al. [31], reported a progressive transformation from T1 to M2 and then to R polymorphs as ZnO content increased. However, these studies did not report furnace type or cooling rates factors known to significantly influence polymorphic stabilization, further complicating direct comparisons.
In addition to single dopant systems, research has also explored the combined effects of dopants such as MgO, Na2O, and SO3. Maki et al. [32] conducted a comprehensive study of industrial clinkers from various regions, concluding that MgO content plays a decisive role in determining the dominant phase in hybrid M1/M3 samples. Subsequent work by Staněk and Sulovský [33] demonstrated that increasing the MgO/SO3 ratio favored stabilization of the M3 polymorph, whereas a lower ratio promoted the M1 form. However, Segata et al. [13] suggested that SO₃ alone can stabilize the M1 polymorph, independent of other impurities.
When evaluating C3S reactivity solely based on polymorphic form, literature commonly ranks the T1 polymorph as the most reactive, followed by M1 and then M3 [17,22,34–38]. Nevertheless, this approach oversimplifies the complex interplay between crystal structure and chemical composition. Minor ionic substitutions originating from raw materials or alternative fuels used in co-processing can significantly alter the local structure and reactivity of C3S. Therefore, a more nuanced understanding of C3S hydration must consider both polymorphism and the role of dopant-induced structural modifications.
Despite these insights, the specific role of dopants in modulating C3S reactivity, independent of polymorphic form, and their influence on both anhydrous and hydrated properties remain insufficiently explored. This study, therefore, seeks to systematically investigate the effect of ionic doping on C3S reactivity using a suite of physicochemical techniques, and to propose a framework for understanding dopant-induced reactivity variations in C3S.
2_Experimental:
Pure tricalcium silicate (C3S) was synthesized using analytical-grade calcium carbonate (CaCO3) and silicon dioxide (SiO2) in a molar ratio of 3:1. For the doped samples, analytical-grade oxides of zinc (ZnO), magnesium (MgO), and titanium (TiO2) were added at concentrations of 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt%, relative to the total mass of the base materials.
The dry components were manually homogenized, and Milli-Q water was gradually added until a paste-like consistency was achieved. The resulting paste was then molded into cylindrical specimens measuring 2.5 cm in diameter and 5.0 cm in height. These specimens were dried at 100 ± 5 °C for 72 h. Following drying, the samples were sintered at 1500 °C for six hours in a muffle furnace. After sintering, the specimens were rapidly cooled to room temperature within a maximum of two minutes using mechanical ventilation to ensure abrupt quenching. Fig. 1  shows the C3S synthesis setup.
The chemical composition of the reagents is shown in Table 2 . These data were obtained commercially from the manufacturers. Specific surface area tests were performed using the BET (Brunauer-Emmett-Teller) method for physical analyses. The equipment used was the Autosorb Quantachrome, model Nova 1000e, which calculates the total surface area of the sample through the adsorbed nitrogen area (m2), based on the volume of adsorbed gas (V) as a function of relative pressure (P/P0). Samples of 1 g of each material investigated were dried at 100 °C for 24 h. Samples of 1 g of each material investigated were dried at 100 °C for 24 h. Particle size distribution of the raw materials was performed on 2 g samples of each reagent in an aqueous medium. A PSA 1090 L Anton-Paar equipment was used for this purpose. 3_Results:
3.1 Particle size distribution (PSD)  Table 4  show the values (including ASS) and particle size distribution curves for the pure and ZnO, TiO2, and MgO-doped phases, respectively. Doping in all samples contributed to an increasing particle size distribution about Dv90. As the dopant content increased, the Dv90 diameter values also increased, requiring greater grinding energy to maintain the finesses parameters compared to reference. The average diameter also showed, for the most part, an increasing behavior as a function of the dopant content used. One can note that the specific surface area decreased, as the dopant content increased. This behavior remains constant for the phases doped with ZnO, indicating a possible formation of less porous agglomerates. However, for the phases doped with TiO2 and MgO, the highest value was found at a content of 0.5 wt%, with 5.280 m2/g and 5.976 m2/g, respectively, and with the increase in dopant content, there was a drastic reduction. This behavior could be associated with greater densification of the sample during sintering.
3.2 Mineralogical composition  Figs. 3 and 4   show the polymorph transition for each phase (pure or doped), with the T3, M1, and M3 polymorphs identified according to the structural models proposed by T3 polymorph (ICSD# 004331 and # 162744), M1 polymorph (ICSD# 81100), M3 (ICSD# 64759), and CaO (ICSD# 75786) and Table 5  shows the percentages for each phase, the stabilized polymorphs, the GOF, and the Rwp. Quantitative phase analysis (Fig. 5 ) revealed that the pure C3S phase consisted predominantly of the triclinic T3 polymorph (98.7 %), with a minor fraction of free lime (f-CaO, 1.3 %). In the ZnO-doped systems, the dominant polymorph shifted toward monoclinic forms. At 0.5 wt% ZnO, the assemblage comprised 92.0 % M1, 6.2 % T3, and 1.9 % f-CaO, whereas at 1.0 wt% ZnO, M1 remained the most abundant phase (68.7 %), accompanied by 29.8 % M3 and 1.5 % f-CaO. For the TiO2-doped compositions, T3 remained predominant, although a partial transition from M1 to T3 was observed at both doping levels. At 0.5 wt% TiO2, the phase distribution was 68.9 % T3, 31.0 % M1, and 0.1 % f-CaO, while at 1.0 wt% TiO2 it was 65.2 % T3, 34.4 % M1, and 0.4 % f-CaO. In MgO-doped samples, T3 and M1 coexisted, with 0.5 wt% MgO yielding 88.7 % T3, 9.5 % M1, and 1.8 % f-CaO, whereas 1.0 wt% MgO produced a more balanced distribution (51.5 % T3, 47.1 % M1, and 1.5 % f-CaO). As the C3S polymorphs are metastable at room temperature, the polymorph with the highest fraction in each doped system was considered the predominant form for this analysis. The T3/M1 and M1/M3 ratios (Fig. 5) indicate that, under the synthesis and cooling conditions employed, T3 tended to stabilize in most cases, except for the 1.0 wt% ZnO system, where monoclinic polymorphs (M1 and M3) predominated, with M1 as the major phase. This divergence may be attributed to the interplay between sintering and cooling protocols and the intrinsic physicochemical characteristics of the dopant cation. Triclinic C3S polymorphs are generally more stable at ambient temperature due to their lower transformation temperatures compared to monoclinic and rhombohedral forms [12,41]. It has been shown that slow cooling or forced ventilation after sintering at 1450–1600 °C favors T3 stabilization [10]. However, the literature indicates that dopant-induced phase stabilization is not straightforward. The phase assemblage depends not only on dopant concentration but also on synthesis temperature, dwell time, and cooling regime, often resulting in the coexistence of multiple polymorphs at room temperature as shown in Table 1. Taken together, these results emphasize the complexity of polymorph stabilization in doped C3S. The observed trends suggest that dopant effects are not governed solely by ionic size or charge, but also by their interaction with the evolving silicate lattice during cooling. A comprehensive understanding of these interactions considering both thermodynamic and kinetic factors is essential to link phase stability to hydration reactivity and, ultimately, to cement performance.
3.3 Effect of doping on the crystal structure  Table 6  presents the physico and chemical properties of the dopants, highlighting that only Mg2+ and Zn2+ possess ionic radio and electronegativity values comparable to Ca2+. This similarity facilitates their incorporation into the C3S structure via substitutional solid solution mechanisms. In contrast, Ti4+ has significantly smaller ionic dimensions and different chemical characteristics, which favors the formation of interstitial solid solutions (Fig. 6 ). This structural behavior is corroborated by the observed amounts of free CaO (f-CaO) in the doped samples: phases doped with MgO exhibit higher f-CaO content compared to those doped with TiO2 (Table 3), suggesting more substantial lattice disruption and limited incorporation. The incorporation of these dopants has a marked impact on the crystal structure and polymorphism of C3S. Mg2+, due to its similar ionic radii and high symmetry, can substitute Ca2+ with minimal disruption to the [SiO4]4− framework. The substitution leads to a decrease in unit cell volume and an increase in crystal density, effectively counterbalancing the higher atomic weight of Mg2+ [42]. Moreover, the presence of Mg2+ influences the enthalpy of formation and promotes polymorphic transitions by inducing structural distortions and increased formation energy, which may ultimately reduce MgO solubility [19,21,42,43]. Experimental and literature data confirm that MgO stabilizes a range of polymorphs, predominantly in the triclinic (T2, T3) and monoclinic (M1, M2) forms, within doping ranges of 0.1 wt%–4.0 wt% [13,19,27,32,42,43]. Similarly, Zn2+ tends to substitute for Ca2+ due to the lower CaO bond energy compared to SiO, leading to lattice contraction. However, Zn incorporation is closely tied to the oxygen vacancy dynamics during sintering, and unlike more volatile elements, ZnO remains stable even at high temperatures [45–49]. Excess Zn not incorporated into the C3S lattice tends to form secondary phases that can alter both reactivity and mechanical strength [18,50]. Importantly, ZnO has been found to stabilize all seven known C3S polymorphs, although no consistent correlation between Zn content and specific polymorph stabilization has been established. Doping levels reported in the literature range from 0.1 wt% to 8.0 wt%, with the polymorphic outcome highly dependent on synthesis conditions. In contrast, the effect of TiO2 on the crystal structure of C3S is less well-defined in the literature. Most studies associate TiO2 with its mineralizing behavior, primarily affecting the liquid phase during sintering. It has been shown to lower the temperature for initial liquid formation, increase melt volume, and enhance reaction kinetics at solid–liquid interfaces [25,52,53]. These phenomena can reduce free CaO and promote C3S formation. However, its incorporation into the C3S crystal structure may be more complex and limited, likely occurring in interstitial positions due to its smaller size and higher charge. Reported polymorphs stabilized by Ti doping include triclinic (T1, T2), monoclinic (M1, M3), and rhombohedral forms, typically at doping levels of 0.5 wt%–2.0 wt% [30,52–55]. Crystallite size. Another significant effect observed in the doped phases is the average crystallite size among the different polymorphs. The pure phase (T3) exhibited the largest crystallite size, while the introduction of dopants influenced this parameter differently depending on the type and content of dopant. Specifically, phases doped with ZnO and MgO showed an increase in crystallite size as the dopant concentration increased, however, for TiO2, a decrease in crystallite size occurred. Table 7  shows the crystallite sizes of each polymorph. This behavior suggests a strong link between dopant type and the diffusion mechanisms active during crystal formation. In the case of ZnO and MgO, the primary diffusion mechanism is associated with oxygen vacancies, which are generated during the substitution of Ca2+ by Zn2+ or Mg2+ in the lattice. These substitutional solid solutions allow the crystal structure to evolve in a manner similar to the pure phase. As the dopant content increases, so does the number of vacancies, which in turn enhances ion mobility and supplies the necessary energy to facilitate bond breaking and dopant incorporation ultimately promoting crystal growth. Additionally, ZnO is known to exhibit anisotropic diffusion behavior [56] which further facilitates directional diffusion and contributes to enhanced crystallite growth. This effect aligns with the observed increase in average crystallite size with ZnO doping. In contrast, TiO2 forms an interstitial solid solution, where the Ti4+ ions occupy positions within the lattice that are not normally occupied by host ions. If no adjustments are made to the synthesis conditions to accommodate this structural disruption, the presence of interstitial ions can impede lattice rearrangement and crystal growth, effectively blocking the expansion of crystallites. This phenomenon is consistent with the mechanism described by Ma et al. [25], in which the incorporation of Ti4+ in interstitial sites leads to structural hindrance and limited crystallite development.
3.4 Molecular change in C3S polymorphism  Fig. 7  shows the behavior of the IR spectra of the C3S polymorphs for the pure and doped phases, and Table 8  shows the vibration bands. The IR absorption spectra formed by C3S can be seen in the 400 to 4000 cm−1 region and present four fundamental vibration modes for the [SiO]4 4− tetrahedra, these being: ν1 symmetrical stretching, ν3 asymmetrical stretching, ν2 in-plane bending and ν4 out-of-plane bending [27,50]. The FTIR spectra of all samples exhibited the characteristic vibrational features of C3S, with band positions and intensities modulated by the type and concentration of dopant. In agreement with previous reports [12,57,58], the undoped C3S phase displayed the symmetric stretching vibration (ν₁) of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra at 860 and 1012 cm −1, asymmetric stretching modes (ν₃) at 1050 and 1008 cm−1, in-plane bending (ν₂) at 492, 461, 434, and 318 cm−1, and out-of-plane bending (ν₄) at 516 cm−1. The prominent band at 862 cm−1 is indicative of the triclinic T3 polymorph, consistent with the XRD phase identification. Doping induced measurable shifts in the main SiO stretching bands, suggesting modifications in the silicate lattice through ionic substitution or localized structural distortion. For both 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt% contents, the ν₃ SiO band shifted slightly toward lower wavenumbers in ZnO-doped and MgO-doped samples compared with TiO2-doped compositions. This downshift is consistent with the larger ionic radii of Zn2+ (0.74 Å) and Mg2+ (0.72 Å) relative to Ti4+ (0.605 Å), which can impose greater lattice strain and alter SiO bond lengths [27,49,50,59]. Similar dopant-induced spectral shifts have been reported for transition-metal-substituted silicates [60], reflecting changes in both bond strength and local symmetry. The bands at 858–860 cm−1, attributed to Si–O–Si bending vibrations [58], exhibited a subtle increase in intensity and a minor shift in samples doped at 1.0 wt%, irrespective of the dopant type. This behavior suggests modifications in intertetrahedral connectivity, potentially linked to dopant–oxygen coordination and charge-balancing mechanisms. In the 400–500 cm−1 region, the observed lower-wavenumber bands correspond to lattice vibrations involving CaO as well as metal–oxygen bonds such as TiO, ZnO, and MgO [27]. The appearance and intensification of these bands in doped samples provide spectroscopic evidence for dopant incorporation into the C3S crystal structure, corroborating the XRD-derived lattice parameter variations. These FTIR findings reinforce the conclusion that the doping strategy adopted in this study effectively promoted partial substitution of Ca2+ sites and altered the silicate framework. The extent and nature of these modifications depended on the dopant ionic radii and valence, as well as on the concentration employed, in line with previous work on doped calcium silicates [10,23,31]. When combined with the crystallographic results, the vibrational spectroscopy data confirm that Zn2+ and Mg2+ exert a more pronounced structural perturbation than Ti4+, potentially influencing both phase stability and hydration reactivity.
3.5 Hydration process  Fig. 8  presents the heat evolution curves of the C3S pastes, both pure and doped, over the first 72 h of hydration. Panels (a) and (b) correspond to 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt% dopant contents, respectively. At a doping content of 0.5 wt%, the MgO-modified C3S phase exhibited the shortest induction period, indicating an earlier onset of hydration. It also presented the highest heat release rate during the acceleration period, with an increase of 34.78 % compared to ZnO (33.81 %), the pure phase (baseline), and TiO2 (70.35 %). When the dopant content was increased to 1.0 wt%, the heat release rate decreased for MgO (29.49 %) and ZnO (20.15 %), whereas TiO2 showed a slight increase (32.43 %). In all cases, MgO and ZnO-doped samples exhibited higher cumulative heat release than both the pure and TiO2 phases. The enhanced early hydration in the MgO series can be attributed to the partial substitution of Mg2+ for Ca2+ within the C3S crystal lattice. Given the ionic radii of Mg2+ (0.72 Å) and Ca2+ (1.00 Å), the ∼28 % difference falls within the Hume–Rothery limit for solid solution formation, allowing substitution with some lattice relaxation [61]. At low substitution levels, this results in a slight lattice contraction, which increases lattice strain energy and facilitates dissolution upon contact with water, enhancing reactivity [41]. However, at higher MgO contents, the accumulation of substitutions can induce localized stress, generating defects such as oxygen or calcium vacancies to relieve strain [12]. This defect formation may reduce structural stability and partially offset the kinetic benefits. In the study of 40 industrial clinkers [62] showed that both periclase content and total MgO in the clinker mineralogy were identified as significant parameters influencing hydration after 7 days. The authors bring to discussion that although the literature remains divided regarding the role of MgO in very early hydration (first 24 h) [63,64], several works [43,65,66] reported that MgO incorporation enhances the degree of hydration at later ages. This effect has been attributed to the incorporation of Mg2+ ions into the C3S lattice, which can accelerate alite hydration rates [66]. Additionally, MgO presence has been linked to the promotion of alite formation during clinker synthesis, indirectly influencing subsequent hydration behavior. Considering the Zn doping, this feature can be explained by the early precipitation of zinc-containing secondary phases, such as Zn(OH)2 [67] or Ca[Zn(OH)3·H2O]3 [68], which sequester Ca2+ from the pore solution and delay its supersaturation, thereby shifting the main C–S–H nucleation event to a later time. The resulting second exothermic peak reflects this delayed growth process. The stabilization of the M1 polymorph in ZnO-doped samples further differentiates their behavior from the T3-based pure and MgO/TiO2 phases, though polymorph stabilization alone does not account for the observed reactivity trends. Indeed, despite all phases except ZnO sharing the T3 polymorph, the reactivity sequence MgO–T3 > pure T3 > TiO2–T3 indicates that catalytic and electronic effects of dopants are more influential than crystal structure alone. The superior reactivity of M1-stabilized ZnO over TiO2–T3 contradicts conventional trends in C3S polymorph reactivity [26,49]. This observation supports the view that foreign ions modify the hydration process primarily through alterations in defect density, local crystal field, and surface chemistry, which in turn modulate dissolution rates and nucleation kinetics [2,10,18,31,42,44,71–74]. Collectively, the results confirm that dopant type and concentration exert a complex, non-linear influence on C3S hydration, arising from the interplay of structural substitution, secondary phase precipitation, and surface-mediated catalytic effects. This reinforces the need to interpret hydration kinetics in doped systems beyond simple polymorph-based frameworks, integrating both bulk and interfacial chemistry effects.
4_Discussion on the catalytic effect:
Catalytic, in the context of cement hydration, refers to the acceleration or retardation of chemical reactions due to the presence of foreign ions or impurities. These species modify the activation energy of the reaction without being consumed and without altering the reaction's equilibrium [75]. Although typically present in low concentrations, dopants can dramatically influence hydration kinetics through structural, chemical, or physical interactions with the host matrix [31,51,71].
4.1 Dopant effects at low concentrations (0.5–1.0 wt%) As shown in Fig. 9 , the dopant type significantly alters the hydration kinetics:  • MgO-doped C3S exhibited the greatest variation in activation energy and the highest cumulative heat release. This behavior is attributed to the formation of structural defects and the inherent high lattice symmetry of MgO, which enhances ionic mobility and facilitates the growth of C-S-H. The dopant likely accumulates at the grain boundaries, enhancing the dissolution rate of C3S and promoting early hydration.   • ZnO-doped C3S, in contrast, showed limited changes in activation energy and lower heat release, indicating sluggish hydration. This aligns with previous reports [18,48,73,76], and is related to ZnO's hexagonal crystal structure and its anisotropic diffusion behavior. Depending on the crystallographic orientation, ZnO may hinder water penetration and Ca2+ diffusion, thereby retarding the reaction.   • TiO2-doped C3S showed an initial reduction in activation energy, suggesting faster onset of hydration. However, the total heat release remained lower than that of the pure phase. This paradox is explained by TiO2's interference in C3S crystal growth during synthesis, which leads to a denser microstructure with reduced pore space for ionic diffusion, limiting long-term hydration despite faster initiation.
4.2 Dopant effects at higher concentrations (4.0–8.0 wt%) The impact of dopant content becomes more pronounced at higher concentrations, as shown in Fig. 10 . Across all dopants, a general reduction in hydration reactivity was observed, marked by delayed induction periods, and diminished heat evolution during the acceleration phase. MgO-doped C3S showed a marked decline in reactivity at 4.0 wt% and 8.0 wt% doping. Although MgO promotes hydration at lower levels, excessive Mg2+ leads to supersaturation and particle agglomeration on the grain surface, forming a barrier that impedes ion exchange. The heat release during the acceleration phase dropped by 74.04 % (4.0 wt%) and 78.28 % (8.0 wt%), with corresponding delays in hydration onset. The early heat release peak observed for the 4.0 wt% ZnO-doped C3S during the dissolution/induction period can be attributed to the rapid reaction of excess Zn2+ ions with OH− in the pore solution, forming secondary phases such as Zn(OH)2. This reaction occurs almost immediately upon mixing with water and releases energy associated with the nucleation of these low-solubility phases. Such behavior has been described by Tao et al. [48] and Gineys et al. [45], who showed that early-stage zinc reactions lead to the formation of insoluble compounds that influence the onset and evolution of cement hydration. ZnO-doped C3S displayed the most dramatic decline in reactivity. At 8.0 wt% ZnO, the induction period extended by ∼30 h, and the acceleration peak nearly vanished. The reduction in reactivity is attributed to the formation of insoluble zinc phases such as Ca[Zn(OH)3·H2O]2 and amorphous Zn(OH)2 during early hydration [48,50,77]. These precipitates scavenge Ca2+ from solution, suppressing supersaturation and delaying C-S-H nucleation. TiO2-doped C3S also showed significant inhibition at higher contents. The 4.0 wt% TiO2 sample exhibited a 91.98 % reduction in acceleration-phase heat release compared to the 0.5 wt% content. At 8.0 wt%, no distinct hydration stages were observed. This is due to the formation of CaTiO3 a stable, unreactive compound that forms a persistent physical barrier on the grain surface, obstructing water ingress and ion mobility.
4.3 Mechanistic summary of catalytic behavior The catalytic effect behavior of each dopant can be rationalized as follows:  •  MgO: Enhances hydration through structural modification. Even at concentrations exceeding solubility limits, hydration proceeds due to reduced unit cell volume and high symmetry. Excess MgO accumulates on the grain surface but remains permeable to ionic diffusion, sustaining hydration.   •  ZnO: Acts as a retarder. At low levels (≤1.0 wt%), Zn2+ reduces C3S reactivity by forming insoluble secondary phases, but hydration is still observable. At higher contents, the precipitation of zinc hydroxides forms a barrier layer that significantly limits Ca2+ availability, halting hydration.   •  TiO  2 : At low content, it reduces activation energy and accelerates initial hydration. However, it disrupts C3S crystallization and forms CaTiO3 during synthesis, which inhibits diffusion during hydration. At higher levels, the surface passivation effect dominates, thereby passivating the surface and halting hydration.    This surface-blocking mechanism is common to all dopants at high concentrations. Excess dopant accumulates at the grain interface, forming a protective layer that impairs ion transport and suppresses C-S-H formation. The magnitude and nature of this barrier depend on the dopant's chemistry, solubility, and interaction with Ca2+ and OH− ions in the pore solution, behavior already observed in the study by Xu et al. [73].
5_Conclusion: This work studied the effect of doping on the reactivity of C3S and its polymorphs, using different techniques and analyzing the properties in the anhydrous and hydrated state. The results indicate:  • The types and contents of dopants used stabilized the T3 and M1 polymorphs at room temperature;   • The type of solid solution formed directly influences the growth of C3S crystals, affecting surface properties and average crystallite size. Substitutional solid solutions tend to generate larger defects with vacancies to relieve substitution stresses, and interstitial solutions can promote grain growth arrest, which will impact average crystallite size;   • The MgO and ZnO dopants, at both doping contents, caused changes in the volume of the unit cell, displacement of the chemical bonds, and orientation in the [SiO]4 4− silicon tetrahedrons;   • C3S doped with MgO showed greater reactivity in the hydration process for both contents when compared to the pure phase and phases doped with ZnO and TiO2;   • The results showed that the doping technique generates a catalytic effect in the hydration process of C3S, with an increase in the energy released and reaction time for the contents of 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt% MgO, and a reduction in the energy released in the phases doped with ZnO and TiO2, regardless of the stabilized polymorph. With the increase in content to 4.0 wt% and 8.0 wt%, a physical barrier is formed, which hinders the diffusion process, making it challenging to form C-S-H. Therefore, the reactivity of C3S cannot be evaluated considering only the forming polymorph.
