1_Introduction: 1.1 Background With the rapid development of China, a great deal of cement is required in civil engineering. In 2017, 2.32 × 1010 tons of cement was produced in China. For 33 consecutive years, China has been ranked first in the world in cement production. The industrial research institute predicted that, in 2018, the amount of cement would reach 2.338 × 1010 tons [1].The rapid developments of cement industry certainly induce a series of environmental problems. Two well-known issues associated with the calcination of cement are the energy consumption and air pollution. To decrease environmental problems without reducing the economic value of cement production, technological methods must be introduced to make more sustainable cement. From literature review, it can be seen that non-traditional cements had been developed by some new methods such as, adding ye’elimite to clinker by the secondary heat treatment [2], direct synthesis of alite-ye’elimite clinker (4.8 wt% ye’elimite) [3,4] and activating belite in belite-sulfoaluminate cement [5,6]. However, few studies have been made to improve the quality of cement by controlling the structure of the phase in cement clinker, especially for alite. Alite is one of the most important mineral phases in cement clinker. It is a kind of solid solution of Ca3SiO5 (C3S) with minor oxides. The amount of alite in cement clinker determines the strength of Portland cement. It is known that Ca3SiO5 exhibits seven polymorphs from room temperature (RT) to 1100 °C: three triclinic polymorphs (T1, T2 and T3), three monoclinic polymorphs (M1, M2 and M3) and one rhombohedral polymorph (R) [7–9]. The phase transformations of C3S are given in the following scheme [10]:    pure:    T   1     ↔   620  ° C     T   2     ↔   920  ° C     T   3     ↔   980  ° C     M   1     ↔   990  ° C     M   2     ↔   1070  ° C   R         doped ( mainly Zn or Mg ) :    M   1     ↔   990  ° C     M   2     ↔   1060  ° C     M   3     ↔   1070  ° C   R      M1 and M3 polymorphs are the most stabilized phases in cement clinker. In the past decade, these two polymorphs were investigated widely. The structure of M3 was solved by Nishi [11]. Mumme [12] extracted and solved an alite single-crystal structure from a clinker and identified the < M> unit cell. Unlike the structure of M3 alite, a superstructure for M1 alite has not been determined. Recently, Noirfontaine [10] presented non-averaged models for the M1 polymorph and reported a set of atomic positions. Courtial [13] used five angular windows in X-ray diffraction patterns to identify M1 or M3 polymorphs. Staněk [14] found that the strength of cements with modified M1 was 10% higher than that of cements with modified M3. Furthermore, the alite polymorphs in cement clinkers was also influenced by the amount of MgO and SO3. As the MgO and SO3 are the most common minor components in cement clinkers [15–17], we begin to notice that the structure modification of clinker phase would be another promising way to enhance the performance of cement. Some researchers started focusing on this part. Li [18,19] investigated the effects of SO3 and MgO on both the formation of cement clinker and the polymorphs of alite. Although lots of works regarding the stabilization of M1 alite by doping MgO and SO3, few focused on the relationships between MgO/SO3 and the M1/M3 ratio in alite, moreover, the relationships between the M1/M3 ratio and the compressive strength. Therefore, this paper aims to investigate the relationship between the SO3/MgO ratio and the M1/M3 ratio in alite, as well as the relationship between the M1/M3 ratio in alite and the compressive strength. Some technique methods such as, X-ray powder diffraction (XRD), High-temperature XRD and Transmission electron microscope (TEM) are used to identify M1- and M3-type alite. In this process, the First-Principles method and quantitative analysis by Rietveld method are also adopted.
2_Experiments:
2.1 Sample preparation Bigare [7] mentioned that the limit for a solid solution of MgO in C3S was 2.0 wt% at 1550 °C. This paper focused on a high content of MgO in alite, so 2.0 wt% of MgO was considered for the alite doping. In Ca3SiO5 (C3S), the Mole ratio of CaO and SiO2 was 3:1. When Mg2+ dissolved into C3S structure, the Ca2+ would be substituted by Mg2+ and cause more free lime formation [20]. When S6+ dissolved into C3S structure, the CaO in CaSO4·2H2O also cause more free lime formation [20]. In order to prevent an increasing content of free lime by doping MgO and SO3, the total mole ratio of (CaO + MgO) and SiO2 was 3:1 during the burdening process. That is to say, when calculating the CaO in raw meal, the doped MgO and CaO in CaSO4·2H2O would be taken into consideration. The loadings of the raw meals are given in Table 1 . Alite samples were synthesized using analytical-grade CaCO3, SiO2, MgO and CaSO4·2H2O (XiLong Scientific). The prepared raw meals (1 kg) were homogenized in a ball mill bottle with ethanol and agate balls for 24 h. Then, the liquid meal was dried and pressed into discs (40 g per disc) for the sintering process. Alite samples were sintered in a resistance furnace. Samples were placed in Pt crucibles, heated at a rate of 10 °C/min to calcination temperature at 1000 °C for 30 min, then heated up to sintering temperature (1500 °C) and held for 6 h. The sintered alites were then cooled with liquid nitrogen.
2.2 Characterization XRD analysis was used to characterize the crystalline structure of the alite and identify the transformation of the polymorphs during the heating process. All samples were finely ground to perform the powder diffraction measurements. The XRD patterns of the samples were collected on a Rigaku SmartLab 3000A diffractometer (Japan) with a Cu Kα radiation source (wavelength = 0.154 nm). The accelerating voltage, accelerating current, and step size of the tests were 40 kV, 20 mA, and 0.02°, respectively. The patterns were collected over a scanning range of 10 - 70° at a speed of 0.5° per minute. High-temperature XRD analysis was performed by a Rigaku SmartLab TM 9 kV diffractometer (Japan) with a Cu Kα radiation source (wavelength = 0.154 nm and without K α2), in which the accelerating voltage, accelerating current, and step size of the tests were 45 kV, 200 mA, and 0.02°, respectively. High-temperature XRD patterns were collected over a scanning range of 10–70° at a speed of 10° per min at each temperature. The heating process was performed at a speed of 10 °C/min. The patterns were collected every 20 °C after the temperature reached 500 °C. The temperature would hold during the XRD data collection Images of the SAED patterns were recorded using TEM (Model JEM-2100UHR, JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. The device was equipped with a double-tilt goniometer, where the maximum tilting angle was ±20° around both the x- and y-axes. The Mumme’s [12] average model (Space group: Cm; a = 1.222 nm, b = 0.708 nm, c = 0.930 nm, α = 90°, β = 114.93°, γ = 90°, Ca18Si6O30, named as pure M3 C3S) have been exported as the initial crystal structure to do the geometry optimization by the first principles calculations which has been performed by CASTEP code [21] based on the density functional theory (DFT [22,23]). Furthermore, different dosages of MgO and SO3 substituted into the above mentioned optimized M3 crystal structures are also investigated by the first principles calculations. Considering the limit of solid solution of MgO and SO3, one S6+ substituted for a Si4+ and Ca2+ (in order to guarantee the conservation of charge, a Ca2+ would be taken away from the structure) and (S6+ + Mg2+) co-substituted Si4+ and Ca2+ were discussed. After substitution, the structural formulae were Ca17Si5SO30 (the content of S6+ was 2.33%) and Ca16MgSi5SO30 (the content of S6+ was 2.36% and the content of Mg2+ was 1.77%). The geometry optimization parameters in CASTEP are demonstrated that the core electrons are treated with the ultrasoft pseudo potential method. The exchange-correlation effects of the valence electrons were described by the generalized gradient approximation (GGA [24]) parameterized by Perdew - Burke - Ernzrhof (PBE [25]) function. The Brillouin zone was sampled with 1 × 2 × 2 k-points using the Monkhorst and Pack method [26] respectively. The energy minimization and action of atomic forces algorithm was the Broyden – Fletcher – Goldfarb - Shanno (BFGS) method [27,28]. An energy cutoff of 340 eV was used for expanding the Kohn-Sham wave functions. The energy convergence criteria were set as follows: the force on the atoms were set to 0.03 eV/Å, the stress on each atom was set to 0.05 GPa, the atomic displacement was less than 0.001 Å and the energy change per atom was set to be less than 1.0e−6 eV. The Cohesive Energy was also calculated and the main steps were followed by Wang [29]. The Rietveld quantitative analysis was performed and the structures used for refinements were: M1 C3S [10], M3 C3S ICSD, No. 64759 [11], β-C2S, ICSD, No. 81096, γ-C2S, ICSD, No. 81095, f-CaO, ICSD, No. 52783 [30], MgO, ICSD, No. 31051 [31], CaSO4, ICSD, No. 1956 [32]. Compressive strength measurements were performed by an AEC-201-type automatic cement strength tester (Wuxi, China). The constant loading rate during compression was 2400 N/s. The specific surface areas of all samples were controlled at 300 ± 20 m2/kg with a 0.26 water/cement ratio (w/c). Cubic paste samples (20 × 20 × 20 mm) were cured at 20 ± 1 °C and 95% relative humidity (RH). Then, the samples were removed from the mould after 1 d and immersed in water at 20 °C until they were utilized for compressive strength testing.
3_Results and discussion:
3.1 M1-type alite identification  3.1.1 XRD analysis at room temperature An exhaustive investigation of the polymorphs of alite was performed using XRD techniques, and the results are illustrated in Figs. 1 and 2  . Li [18] had reported nine characteristic windows in the XRD patterns that can be used to distinguish M1 alite from M3 alite in cement clinker. Here, six of the nine windows in Li’s article were chosen to distinguish between the M1 alite and M3 alite after doping with MgO and SO3. Compared the windows W2, W4, W5 and W6 in Fig. 2 with the same area mentioned in reference [18] (Especially the peak between 36.5° and 37° in W5, M3 alite had the characteristic peak at about 36.7° while this peak was not appeared in M1 alite), Blank, 0.5%, and 1.0% SO3 samples were identified as M3 alite. The peak at approximately 25.5° in W1 and two peaks in W2 were only observed in M1 that was obtained after doping with both MgO and SO3 [18]. So, 1.5%, 2.0% and 2.5% SO3 samples were determined to produce M1 alite. Meanwhile, W4 and W6 show the fingerprint areas of C3S [7,9]. Taylor [15] had reported the XRD patterns of the fingerprint regions for C3S with different modifications. By comparing the obtained patterns with the fingerprint regions in reference [15], Blank, 0.5%, and 1.0% SO3 samples corresponded to M3 alite, while 1.5%, 2.0% and 2.5% SO3 samples corresponded to M1, as mentioned before.   3.1.2 High-temperature XRD analysis To investigate the fingerprint regions of M1 C3S at high temperature, a pure C3S sample was heated from room temperature (RT) to 1100 °C. The test methods and instrument used are given in the Characterization section. The fingerprint regions at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 3 , and the XRD pattern at 980 °C is shown in Fig. 4 . From Fig. 3, we could determine that the polymorphs of pure C3S at room temperature were T1 and T2 at 620 °C, T3 at 900 °C, M1 at 960 °C, M2 at 1000 °C and R at 1100 °C, which match results previously reported by Bigare [7]. During the heating process, the polymorph of M3 was not found in the XRD patterns, which corresponded with Noirfontaine [10].  Fig. 4 shows the XRD pattern of pure C3S at 980 °C, and an M1-type polymorph could be identified from the fingerprint area. This pattern was the same as the patterns of samples doped with 1.5%, 2.0% and 2.5% SO3, which confirmed the polymorphs of them (samples doped with 1.5%, 2.0% and 2.5% SO3) were M1 on the other side.   3.1.3 TEM To further resolve the M1-type and M3-type alite at the microscale, the 1.0% SO3 sample and the 1.5% SO3 sample were examined by TEM. The test methods and instrument used are given in the Characterization section. The SAED patterns were calculated using the computer programme SingleCrystal (CrystalMaker Software Ltd., U.K.). The fingerprint area of the XRD patterns from Ca17Si5SO30 and Ca16MgSi5SO30 were given in Fig. 8  and it was found that the fingerprint area was similar to the 1.5% SO3 sample, which was given in Fig. 2 (W4 and W6). Notably, the TEM showed that alite with this kind of fingerprints tended to be M1-type. According to the structural simulation using First-Principles Calculations, doping with MgO and SO3 could change the M3-type alite to an M1-type. The calculated energies of pure M3 C3S, Ca17Si5SO30 and Ca16MgSi5SO30 are shown in Table 2 . The Delta Cohesive Energies of Ca17Si5SO30 and Ca16MgSi5SO30 were similar, and over 10 eV higher than pure M3 C3S which indicated that the polymorphs of Ca17Si5SO30 and Ca16MgSi5SO30 were different from pure M3 C3S. This result is consistent with the previously discussed results from the simulated XRD.
3.2 Quantitative analysis Li [19] reported the correlation between SO3/MgO and C3S composition in cement clinker, but the correlation between SO3/MgO and the composition of M1 type alite was not mentioned. During the formation of alite doped with MgO and SO3, part of the S6+ was volatilized and part of the S6+ was doped into C3S. This would lead to an inhomogeneous distribution of S6+ in the resultant alite. M1-type and M3-type alite would also be coexistent. To correlate the SO3/MgO to the composition of the M1-type alite, quantitative analyses of the samples were calculated by the Rietveld method. Several examples of Rietveld refinements are shown in Fig. 9 , and the complete results are given in Table. 3 .  Fig. 10  shows the variations in the phase composition with increasing SO3/MgO. The increasing content of SO3 promoted the formation of M1-type alite and the transformation of γ-C2S into β-C2S. The content of C3S, C2S and f-CaO depended on the dosage of SO3. Low dosages of SO3 accelerated the reaction of C2S and CaO to form C3S, while excessive amounts of SO3 caused the decomposition of C3S. An optimal content of SO3 that could provide a maximized C3S content could certainly be determined. Nonlinear fittings were used to analyse the results. The equations used for the fitting are given in Fig. 11 , and the modelled results were in good agreement with the experimental data.
3.3 Compressive strength Because the compressive strength is an important index that reflects the properties of fresh and hardened cement pastes, the influence of the SO3 in alite with a high content of MgO on the compressive strengths at different ages is further investigated, as shown in Fig. 12 . When the SO3 was below a certain value, the compressive strengths at different ages increased with increasing SO3. However, when the SO3 exceeded that value, the compressive strengths decreased with increased SO3. This could be explained by the decomposition of C3S. Combined with the content of C3S, when the samples had a similar content of C3S (such as the 2.0% SO3 sample and the 1.0% SO3 sample, see Table. 3), the one with the larger content of M1 alite would have a greater compressive strength. Furthermore, the corresponding increase in ratios as listed in Fig. 12, a similar trend in the development of compressive strength can be clearly observed. However, the increase in the ratio decreases with the curing age. For the sample with 1.5% SO3, the ratio increases to as high as 36.0% after 1 d of curing, while the increased ratio decreases back down to 9.5% after 28 d. These results indicate that the effect of SO3 addition on the early development of strength is significant. To help predict the compressive strength of the clinker at a later time, a relationship between M1% in alite, SO3/MgO and compressive strength was established. Nonlinear fitting was used to simulate the curve, and it was found that a cubic polynomial (y = a + bX + cX2 + dX3) perfectly fit the curve. The fitting information is given in Figs. 13  and Fig. 14 . The optimal M1% in alite was approximately 68% and the best SO3/MgO ratio was approximately 0.43 because the compressive strength could be maximized at each age.
4_Conclusions:
The results show that in low doses, SO3 promotes the formation of alite. If overdosed, however, SO3 will lead to the decomposition of alite, which is the primary factor for the decreased compressive strength of alite with a high SO3 content.
The TEM results show that M1 alite has an incommensurate modulated structure feature with 2.4 times the subcell dimension along [    2   ¯     10]H ∗ and could be expressed as ha∗ + kb∗ + lc∗ + m/[2.4(−2a∗ + b∗)], where m = ±1. The characteristic XRD patterns (fingerprint region) of alite doped with MgO and SO3 were determined by X-ray powder diffraction at both room temperature and high temperature. The simulated structure of M1 alite was calculated using the First-Principles method and the Delta Cohesive Energy between M1 and M3 alite is approximately 11–12 eV.

Title: Studies on the formation and hydration of tricalcium silicate doped with CaF2 and TiO2
Abstract: The comprehensive utilization of wasted pickling sludge in the cement kiln would be a promising practice, but the calcination process of cement clinker became complicated due to the simultaneous introduction of titanium and fluorine. In this paper, the formation and hydration of tricalcium silicate (C3S) doped with CaF2 and TiO2 were discerned by XRD, FT-IR, XPS and isothermal calorimetry. The results revealed that the addition of CaF2 more than 1.5% would promote the appearance of CaTiO3 as the indicator of the solution limit of TiO2, and the formation of CaTiO3 and β-C2S was a concomitant process as the solution limit of TiO2 reached. The addition of 0.5% TiO2 and some addition of CaF2 (≤1.5%) would reduce the polymorph symmetry of C3S, while more addition of CaF2 and TiO2 would actualize the higher polymorph symmetry from M1 to R form. The IR spectra for the polymorphs (T3, M3, R + M3, R) became broader with the increase of the polymorph symmetry of C3S. The replacement of O2− by F− would not be interfered by the simultaneous introduction of titanium, a Ti2p 1/2 peak at 463.39 eV reflected the solution of titanium in the structure of C3S, and the defect reactions of the doped C3S with CaF2 and TiO2 were proposed. The doped C3S had a higher heat flow than the undoped C3S in the initial period, the more addition of CaF2 inhibited the initial hydration activity of C3S, while the addition of TiO2 improved the effect. The incorporation of TiO2 into the doped C3S aggravated the retardation effect caused by CaF2 on the hydration in the acceleration period. The dopant types displayed a more distinct effect than the types of C3S polymorphs on the hydration activity of C3S.
1_Introduction:
An exponential population growth, a rapid urbanization and a remarkable infrastructure volumes have boosted incrementally the generation of municipal and industrial solid wastes. World Bank Project counted the production of municipal solid waste to reach approximately 2.6 million tons by the end of 2025 [1]. Synchronously, industrial solid wastes such as oil-based mud from oil-well drilling [2], iron ore tailings [3], dam fine sediment from marine dredging operations [4], vitrified medical wastes bottom ash [5], waste gypsum [6], spent catalyst [7], spent activated carbon of potabilization plants [8], and various post-industrial wastes [9] were ceaselessly emerging with great quantities, the contamination issues engendered by disposing these wastes has triggered far-reaching concerns. The global cement production was over 5.0 billion tons in 2018 and still drifting upward [10], it might make the cement industry become a promising alleviation for these disposal issues. The cement kiln co-processing technology has been extensively concerned by many researchers from various countries [11–15], this waste treatment practice is becoming more universal for high reaction temperatures over 1000 °C, long residence times, good turbulence and mixing conditions [16,17]. However, these industrial and municipal wastes generally contained a certain amount of heavy metals and some other impurities, it would shift or degrade the multiple properties of the produced clinker [18,19]. The persuasive investigations and the sufficient researches would be necessary before applying this utilization in practice. To reinforce the rationality and applicability of co-processing different wastes in the cement kiln, a number of explorations about the doping effects by the various elements on the cement clinkers kept unfolding.
Exemplifying the waste pickling sludge generated from the manufacturing of titanium and titanium alloy, and plenty of hydrofluoric acid, as one of the effective pickling solvent, were employed to remove the stains and residual oxide film on the surface of the titanium products [20]. The waste pickling sludge would be generated by a series of technological processes. To realize the proper application of these waste pickling sludge as one part of reutilized resource, co-processing the waste pickling sludges as part of raw meal in cement kiln could be a promising practice. However, the incorporation of the waste pickling sludge into the cement raw meal would result in the increased complexity of calcination progress due to the simultaneous introduction of titanium and fluorine.
CaF2 was recognized as the most experimented mineralizer and flux, it could not only stimulate the cement clinker formation, but also lessen energy consumption during cement clinker sintering [21–22]. For a given clinkering temperature range from 1200 °C to 1450 °C, the addition of fluorite (CaF2) in the raw meal could promote the formation of C3S and improve the burnability and lower clinkering temperatures of oxide melts by 50–100 °C. The solid-state diffusion would be enhanced, the viscosity and surface tension of the liquid-state could be also reduced [21–26]. But it had a slight effect on the decomposition of calcite [27]. The NMR findings expounded that the fluoride anions are preferentially incorporated into the alite structure in substitution of the O2− not linked to silicon [28], and the substitution of free O2− by F− will lead to an excess of positive charge which have to be compensated by as much calcium vacancies [29–30]. Guan et al. [31] demonstrated that one defect reaction would present as fluoride anions were incorporated into the C3S structure:   Ca  F 2   →  C 3 S   2  F O ·  +  V  Ca  ″  + C  a  Ca    . The results indicated that the pure C3S had the lowest symmetry with a triclinic form T, but the polymorph of C3S doped with 1.0 wt% CaF2 came to be a monoclinic form M1, the polymorph of C3S transformed into rhombohedral form R with 2.0 wt% CaF2 doping [31]. Kacimi et al. [32] revealed that the presence of F− accelerated the formation of alite and altered the original morphology and the crystal size of alite, besides, the high alite content and its disturbed crystal lattice induced by F− introduction could improve the clinker hydraulic reactivity. Emanuelson et al. [33] once pointed that the improved hydraulic activity of mineralised clinker was caused by the introduction of defects with substitutions rather than a change in polymorph symmetry of alite. It was clarified that the decreased hydraulic activity of the mineralised clinker could be attributed to the high levels of fluoride, 0.4 wt% F, it might originate from the formation of insoluble barrier layers on the surface of the clinker minerals. Therefore, to realize the proper performance of resulted clinkers, the maximum incorporation level of fluoride should be approximately 0.25–0.6% (0.5–1.2% CaF2) by weight [26,34–35].
TiO2 in a moderate addition would affect acid based equilibrium [MeO4]5− and [MeO5]9− in the clinker melt to make the viscosity of melt lower and the surface tension higher [18,19]. Both cases could accelerate the assimilation/binding of lime and favor the crystallization of clinkering reactants [19]. Katyal et al [36] once pointed that the introduction of TiO2 could change the polymorphic form of tricalcium silicate differently in different additions: Up to 2.0% TiO2, triclinic form, 4.0–5.0% TiO2, monoclinic form, and 6.0% TiO2, rhombohedral form. It was ascertained that TiO2 would be incorporated into C3S up to 4.5% at 1450 °C and beyond this limit a new phase CaO·TiO2 would form. For hydration process, the presence of small quantity of TiO2 could enhance the hydraulic activity of cement clinker, it could be attributed to the lattice distortion of alite and belite crystal caused by the substitution of the Si4+ ion by Ti4+ ion and the formation of corresponding solid solutions [30]. Katyal et.al [37] also revealed that introduction of TiO2 into C3S affected the hydraulicity of C3S by modifying the polymorphism of C3S and forming a CaO·TiO2 compound. The presence of up to 2.0% TiO2 slowed down the hydration process for about 2 days and then picked up to exceed the degree of hydration of undoped C3S. Higher percentages of TiO2 above 2.0% showed a higher hydration rate from 1 h to 28 d. Shang et al. [38] reported that TiO2-doped could accelerate the hydration activity of clinker in the initial period while postponed the hydration of C3S in the later period, and after hydration of 28 d, C-S-H gel polymerization degree improved by introduction of TiO2 less than 1.5% by mass. Beyond it, the polymerization degree came to reduce.
Though these existing findings have demonstrated the single effect of CaF2 or TiO2 on the formation and hydration performances of clinker minerals, the studies regarding the co-doping effects of CaF2 and TiO2 on the formation of clinker minerals were scare, and its effects on the properties of clinker minerals also need further study. These all are the essential parts to evaluate the feasibility of co-processing the pickling sludge in the cement kiln. Therefore, this study would concentrate on tricalcium silicate (C3S) to identify the formation and hydration of C3S doped with CaF2 and TiO2. The formation of C3S and the polymorphs of C3S were investigated by XRD. The characteristics of IR spectra of C3S doped with CaF2 and TiO2 were discussed. The chemical valence states of fluorine and titanium in the doped C3S was determined by XPS, and the effect of CaF2 and TiO2 on the hydration activity of C3S was explored by isothermal heat flow calorimeter.
2_Materials and methods:
2.1 Material preparation The undoped and doped C3S samples were synthesized by a conventional solid-state sintering method. The analytical grade chemical reagents SiO2, CaCO3, CaF2, and TiO2 were regarded as the starting materials. Table 1  provided the detailed compositions of the different doped C3S samples. It should be noted that the redundant calcium from the introduction of CaF2 into the doped C3S samples would interfere the final form of C3S, so the brought calcium by CaF2 should be taken off from the CaCO3 content. The addition of TiO2 would be based on the total mass of CaCO3 and SiO2, and was not affected by the addition of CaF2. The previously dried 1.0 mol SiO2 and 3.0 mol CaCO3 powders with or without the different types and dosages of dopants were homogenized for 3 h in a small-scale powder mixer. The mixtures were then mixed with deionized water again for 0.5 h and pressed into cylindrical pellets at 40.0 MPa. The pellets were sintered in a tubular high temperature furnace XCSL-16–17 V with the successive sintering procedures in Table 2 . The air-quenched sintered samples would be reground to powders, pelletized and sintered using the same sintering procedures until a less than 0.1% (wt. %) free lime content of the sintered samples reached.
2.2 Analytical techniques The free lime contents of the doped C3S samples were analyzed by the ethanol-glycol method using F Ca-2008 free lime measuring instrument. All the mineral X-ray diffraction of the undoped and doped C3S samples were measured by X-Ray diffraction (XRD, a Bruker D8 Advance) in the 5°–65° (2θ) with CuKα1,2 (λ1 = 0.15406 nm, λ2 = 0.15444 nm) at 40 KV and 40 mA. The procedures of smoothing, background deducting and Kα stripping were implemented on the all raw XRD patterns. The full XRD data was collected over 5°–65° with 0.02° step width and 1.0 s step time. The regional XRD data in the range of 31.5°–33° and 51°–52.5° was rescanned with 0.003° step width and 1.0 s step time. Bruker Vertex 70 Fourier transform infrared spectrometer was used to measure the FT-IR spectra of some doped C3S samples among the region 400 cm−1–4000 cm−1 at a spectral resolution of 4 cm−1. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was carried out by using a Thermo ESCALAB 250XI photoelectron spectrometer fitted with Mg Kα (hν = 1253.6 eV) X-ray source operating at 16 KV, 14.9 mA. A small portion of the doped C3S samples was ground into fine powders (less than 75 μm) and pressed into a stainless steel sample holder. The pass energies of survey and narrow spectra were 100 eV and 30 eV. The measured data would be extracted from the XPS spectra via a Thermo Avantage Version 5.976 software. A Shirley background was assumed in the all cases. The XPS spectra was corrected for the charging effects by the adventitious carbon peak C1s line at a BE = 284.8 eV. The spectra retrieval was proceeded with built-in XPS Knowledge View in Thermo Avantage software and NIST X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy Database (website available: https://srdata.nist.gov/xps/Default.aspx) [39]. The developments of heat flow and total hydration heat of the doped C3S samples were monitored by the TAM Air isothermal calorimetry. The selected samples were ground to pass 75 μm sieve, and the calorimetric measurements were proceeded at 25 °C for 7 d with w/c = 0.5. The samples were well mixed with water and stirred outside the calorimeter using a homemade mixer. The measurement would start 1 min after the mixing procedure.
3_Results and discussion:
3.1 XRD analysis of doped C3S samples The full XRD pattern analysis was carried out to identify the effects of CaF2 and TiO2 on the formation of C3S under the different doping conditions. The results were presented in Fig. 1  (a–m) and Table 3 . The regional XRD patterns in the range of 31.5°–33° and 51°–52.5° were the important fingerprint-regions of the symmetries of different C3S polymorphs [40–42]. The various C3S polymorphs (T1, T2, T3, M1, M3 and R) would be determined by the characteristic peaks referring to the existing researches [41–46]. The built-in illustrations in Fig. 1 (a–m) showed the two selected regions, and the main information of the C3S polymorphs under the different doping conditions were summarized in Table 3. The phase compositions of different doped C3S samples indicated that the addition of CaF2 from 1.0% to 2.0% would not interfere the formation of C3S phase, but the CaF2 and TiO2 exhibited a distinct effect on the formation of C3S phase. The appearance of CaTiO3 would indicate the solution limit of TiO2 in the doped C3S samples, and the solution limit of TiO2 appeared earlier compared with the Katyal’s findings [36]. The addition of 1.0% CaF2 and 2.0% TiO2 could make the solution limit of TiO2 appear, while the addition of 1.5% or 2.0% CaF2 and 1.0% TiO2 could make the solution limit of TiO2 appear. Hence, the prior solution of CaF2 in the doped C3S would accelerate the appearance of the solution limit of TiO2. It could be observed that the formation of CaTiO3 was accompanied with the formation of β-C2S, it implied the formation reaction of CaTiO3 would assimilate the CaO from the reaction between C2S and CaO, and the stronger diffraction intensity of CaTiO3 with the doping addition of CaF2 and TiO2 increasing also indicated that the addition of CaF2 would be adverse to the solution of TiO2 in the doped C3S. In Table 3, It could be noticed that the pure C3S had the lowest symmetry with triclinic form T3, three characteristic peaks were detected between 31.5° and 33°, three characteristic peaks were detected between 51° and 52.5°, and the last two peaks between 51° and 52.5° had a tendency to merge [43]. The doped C3S with 1.0% CaF2 was determined as the polymorph coexistence of T3 and M1, the main phase could be identified as M1-type C3S [41–42]. The doped C3S with 1.0% CaF2 and 0.5% TiO2 had the same feature as sample F1, but the characteristic peaks between 51° and 52.5° was more close the T3-type C3S [43]. It might mean that the doping addition of 1.0% CaF2 and 0.5% TiO2 would lower the symmetry of C3S. The doped C3S with 1.0% CaF2 and 1.0% TiO2 presented the M1-type C3S, and the doped C3S with 1.0% CaF2 and 2.0% TiO2 presented the M3-type C3S [42,46]. The doped C3S with 1.5% CaF2 presented the polymorph coexistence of T3 and M1, the main phase would be identified as M1-type C3S, and the feature of T3-type C3S nearly disappeared. Although the doped C3S with 1.5% CaF2 and 0.5% TiO2 also showed the polymorph coexistence of T3 and M1, the characteristic peaks between 51° and 52.5° came to be more similar as T3-type C3S than sample F2. The relative low addition of TiO2 (<0.5%) might disorganize the formation of C3S polymorphs doped with CaF2 to make the structure characteristics of T3-type C3S more measurable, in other words, the relative low addition of TiO2 might promote the presence of the superstructure of T3-type C3S along with the reduction in polymorph symmetry [47]. The doped C3S with 1.5% CaF2 and 1.0% TiO2 showed the M3-type C3S. The characteristic peaks between 31.5° and 33° of the doped C3S with 1.5% CaF2 and 2.0% TiO2 came to merge to two peaks, it was pivotal to identify the R-type C3S [36,43], and the peaks between 51° and 52.5° showed M3-type C3S, it exhibited the polymorph coexistence of R and M3. The doped C3S with 2.0% CaF2 came to present M3-type C3S, and the doped C3S with 2.0% CaF2 and 0.5% TiO2 showed the same polymorphs as sample F2T2. The C3S polymorphs with the addition of 2.0% CaF2 and 0.5% TiO2 was different from the doped C3S with 1.0% or 1.5% CaF2, it could be found that the doping addition of 0.5% TiO2 and 2.0% CaF2 was useful to promote the transformation from low symmetry polymorph to high symmetry polymorph of C3S. Both Sample F3T1 and F3T2 had the typical features of R-type C3S: two characteristic peaks were between 31.5° and 33° and one characteristic peak was between 51° and 52.5°. It could be concluded that the addition of CaF2 from 1.0% to 2.0% was beneficial to elevate the symmetry of C3S polymorph compared with the undoped C3S, while the co-doping addition of CaF2 and TiO2 would increase the complexity of C3S polymorphs. Incorporating 0.5% TiO2 into the doped C3S with 1.0% or 1.5% CaF2 would reduce the symmetry of C3S polymorph to some extent. It could be noticed that the co-doping of CaF2 and TiO2 had the more positive influence on the symmetry of C3S polymorphs compared with that doped with CaF2.
3.2 IR spectra analysis of doped C3S samples The various C3S polymorphs were very similar to each other in terms of the atomic site occupation of the calcium cation, oxygen ion and silicon cation, only the orientation of [SiO4]4− tetrahedra presented some differences [40]. The IR absorption bands of the doped C3S sample in the range of 400–1400 cm−1 could be mainly caused by the vibration of [SiO4]4− tetrahedron, and the isolated [SiO4]4− tetrahedra consisted of four vibration modes, including symmetric stretching vibration (ν1), asymmetric stretching vibration (ν3), in-plane bending vibration (ν2) and out-plane bending vibration (ν4) [43].  Fig. 2  (a–c) provided the IR spectra of different doped C3S, and the information of various vibration bands were listed in Table 4 . The main vibrations of the undoped C3S sample had no symmetric stretching vibration (ν1), but had the asymmetric stretching vibration (ν3) at 937 and 890 cm−1, in-plane bending vibration (ν2) at 454 cm−1 and out-plane bending vibration (ν4) at 524 cm−1, it could imply that the polymorph of undoped C3S would be a T3-type C3S. This result was also demonstrated by Ren, De la Torre and Peterson that the sharp symmetric stretching vibration of T3-type C3S at approximately 812 cm−1 would vanish differing from T1-type or T2-type C3S [43,48,49]. The main vibrations of sample F1 and F1T0 were similar, only some small shifts of the in-plane bending and asymmetric stretching vibration could be observed. But sample F1T2 showed a distinct change at 751 and 728 cm−1 symmetric stretching vibration, it was corresponding to the characteristic vibration of Metal-Oxygen (M−O) bond [50], and the presence of CaTiO3 just indicated the existence of Ti-O bond. The asymmetric stretching vibration at 751 and 728 cm−1 could conform to the characteristic of Ti-O vibrational mode as well [51]. The vibration modes of the doped system with 1.5% CaF2 were similar to that with 1.0% CaF2, the symmetric stretching vibration of sample F2T2 also confirmed the existence of Ti-O bond. The formation of CaTiO3 and β-C2S could be a concomitant process analyzed by Section 3.1, the characteristic IR spectra of β-C2S in sample F1T2 and F2T2 was not observed, and it might be due to the interference of the phase contents and sample sampling. The vibration modes of the doped system with 2.0% CaF2 were similar to that with 1.5% CaF2, but the asymmetric stretching vibration at 751 and 846 cm−1 was different, the asymmetric stretching vibration at 846 cm−1 was corresponding to a characteristic vibration spectra of β-C2S [51]. It could be found that there were only minor changes in the IR spectra of all the doped C3S samples due to the fact that the IR spectra of higher symmetry polymorphs M1, M3 and R are similar to that of T3 [43]. Meanwhile, IR spectra of sample Control, F1T2, F2T2 and F3T2 were observed that the characteristic peaks for the polymorphs (T3, M3, R + M3, R) became broader with the increase of the polymorph symmetry of C3S, it was also reported by Ren [43]. In addition, the asymmetric stretching vibration of sample Control, F1T2, F2T2 and F3T2 presented a consistent shift to lower wave numbers, it might be originated from the increase of the polymorph symmetry of C3S. However, to understand the effect of CaF2 and TiO2 on the atomic site occupation of the structure of C3S, the more in-depth researches still need to be put forward.
3.3 XPS analysis of doped C3S samples XPS would provide the binding energies (BE) of the core-level electronic states of the elements in the surface region, and the valuable information concerning the elements could effectively explain the binding situation of key elements [52]. To explore the chemical valence states of fluorine and titanium in the doped C3S, the binding energies of fluorine and titanium were investigated by XPS narrow spectrum using Gaussian Fitting method. Fig. 3  (a–b) showed XPS survey spectrum and narrow spectrum of F1s for the doped C3S with 2.0% CaF2. Fig. 4  (a–c) showed XPS survey spectrum, F1s narrow spectrum and Ti2p narrow spectrum for the doped C3S with 2.0% CaF2 and 2.0% TiO2. In Fig. 3 (a), the major surface components were Ca, Si, C (due to the C pollution), O and F. Fig. 3 (b) showed the only one Gaussian Fitting peak of F1s at 685.05 eV, it was corresponding to the F− of CaF2 according to the spectra retrieval [39]. The absence of CaF2 in the doped C3S with 2.0% CaF2 hinted the solution of F in the structure of C3S, and the F− would replace some O2− to bind Ca2+. The replacement of O2− by F− would cause an excess of positive charge, it would be made up by the calcium vacancies [29–30]. The defect reaction:   Ca  F 2   →  C 3 S   2  F O ·  +  V  Ca  ″  + C  a  Ca     pointed by Guan [31] would promote the understanding of the replacement of O2− by F−. In Fig. 4 (a), the major surface components were Ca, Si, C (due to the C pollution) and O, the components of F and Ti were relatively minor due to the sintering uniformity and detection depth limit of XPS. The XPS narrow spectrum of F1s and Ti2p also could give necessary information by Gaussian Fitting. Fig. 4 (b) presented one main Gaussian Fitting peak of F1s at 684.63 eV, it was also corresponding to the F− of CaF2 according to the spectra retrieval [39]. The finding indicated that in the doped C3S with CaF2 and TiO2, the binding situation of fluorine would not be interfered by the addition of TiO2. Fig. 4 (c) presented two main Gaussian Fitting peak at 458.18 eV (Ti2p 3/2) and 463.39 eV (Ti2p 1/2), the Ti2p 3/2 peak at 458.18 eV was corresponding to the Ti-O of CaTiO3 using the spectra retrieval [39], and the Ti2p 1/2 peak at 463.39 eV was corresponding to the Ti-O of TiO2 using the spectra retrieval [39]. It could be noticed that the Ti-O of CaTiO3 would be consistent with the XRD analysis, and another Ti-O of TiO2 could be an evidence of titanium solution in the structure of C3S. The Ti4+ could substitute Si4+ of [SiO4]4− tetrahedra, and the substitution of Si4+ by Ti4+ would keep the charge balance, the finding could be verified by several researches [30,36]. The defect reaction could be regarded as follows:   Ca  F 2  + T i  O 2   →  C 3 S   T  i  Si   + 2  F O ·  +  V  Ca  ″  + 2  O O  + C  a  Ca    .
3.4 Hydration heat evolution of doped C3S samples It was once reported by Stewart et al. that C3S with different polymorphs showed different hydration performance in the early hydration, and the sequence of hydration reactivity was: M−type > T-type > R-type [53]. Zhou et al. and Staněk et al. further conducted the related studies [54–55], however, these findings were not consistent due to the different doping conditions. In this study, the isothermal calorimeter was used to investigate the effect of CaF2 and TiO2 on the hydration activity of the doped C3S (in Fig. 5  and Fig. 6 ). The hydration of C3S exhibited the typical four periods: initial period, induction period, acceleration period and deceleration period, and these periods could be observed within 24 h [40,56]. A rapid heat flow could be noticed within 0.5 h in the initial period. The sequence of heat flow from rapid to slow in the initial period would be: F3T2 > F1 > F2 > F2T0 > F3 > Control. The doped C3S showed a higher heat flow than the undoped C3S in the initial period, the increased addition of CaF2 presented a negative effect on the initial hydration of C3S (dissolution process), while the addition of TiO2 would reverse the negative effect caused by the addition of CaF2. The more addition of TiO2 would present more rapid initial hydration, and 0.5% addition of TiO2 could reduce the initial hydration of the doped C3S with 1.5% addition of CaF2. It was once reported by Katyal [37] that the presence of TiO2 up to 2.0% had an inhibiting effect on the rate of hydration C3S, but the findings of this study seems to demonstrate that the synergistic addition of CaF2 and TiO2 into C3S might enhance the dissolution of the doped C3S in the initial period hydration. The promoted initial hydration activity of the doped C3S might stem from the increased defects of the doped C3S structure [30]. The induction period of the doped C3S was prolonged obviously compared with the undoped C3S, and the induction period of the doped C3S with 2.0% CaF2 and 2.0% TiO2 was prolonged to approximately 40 h, it might mainly result from the formation of low cementitious CaTiO3 and β-C2S [37]. The appearing time of acceleration period from early to last would be: Control, F1, F2, F2T0, F3 and F3T2. The heat flow of the acceleration period were evidently slowed down, as a result, the main formation process of C-S-H gel would be retarded, and the incorporation of TiO2 into the doped C3S with CaF2 would aggravate the retardation of the hydration in the acceleration period. The retardation mechanism was once revealed by the hypothesis that special foreign ions would generate a least soluble barrier layers, it could precipitate onto the surface of hydrated C3S to retard the further hydration [33,57]. The total hydration heat of the doped C3S in Fig. 6 also characterized the positive effect of the addition of CaF2 and TiO2 on the initial hydration of C3S, but the negative effect on the later periods. It could be found that the dopant types displayed the more obvious effect than the types of C3S polymorphs on the hydration activity of C3S. However, more investigations should be carried out to prove the validity of above hypothesis or other retardation mechanism of the obtained findings.
4_Conclusions: The conclusions might be drawn from the present research as follows:  1. A certain addition of CaF2 would accelerate the appearance of the solution limit of TiO2 to generate CaTiO3 in the doped C3S. The formation of CaTiO3 and β-C2S was a concomitant process as the solution limit of TiO2 reached.   2. The pure C3S had the lowest symmetry with a triclinic form T3, and the addition of TiO2 and CaF2 would make the transformation process of polymorph complicated. The addition of 0.5% TiO2 and the addition of 1.0% or 1.5% CaF2 would lead to the reduction of C3S polymorph symmetry, however more addition of CaF2 and TiO2 could actualize the change to the higher polymorph symmetry of C3S. The co-doping addition of CaF2 and TiO2 generally could promote the polymorphic transformation of C3S from low symmetry to higher symmetry.   3. There were only minor changes in the IR spectra of the different doped C3S samples, and the IR spectra of the selected samples with different polymorphs (T3, M3, R + M3, R) were observed that the characteristic peaks for the polymorphs became broader with the increase of the polymorph symmetry of doped C3S.   4. In the doped C3S, the binding situation of fluorine would not be interfered by the introduction of titanium. The appearance of Ti2p 1/2 peak at 463.39 eV proved the solution of titanium in the structure of C3S, and the defect reaction of could be regarded as:   Ca  F 2  + T i  O 2   →  C 3 S   T  i  Si   + 2  F O ·  +  V  Ca  ″  + 2  O O  + C  a  Ca    .   5. The doped C3S showed a higher heat flow than the undoped C3S in the initial period, but the increased addition of CaF2 presented a negative effect on the initial hydration of C3S. The addition of TiO2 weakened the above effect, and more addition of TiO2 would present more rapid initial hydration rate. However, the heat flow of the doped C3S in the acceleration period was evidently slowed down, and the incorporation of TiO2 into the doped C3S would aggravate the retardation effect caused by CaF2 in the acceleration period. The results from hydration heat evolution revealed that the dopant types show a more distinct effect than the types of C3S polymorph on the hydration activity of C3S.

Title: Unveiling the cooperation effects of fluorine and copper on tricalcium silicate (C3S) during cement kiln co-processing hazardous wastes containing Cu
Abstract: Fluorine (F) from fluorite mineralizer and copper (Cu) would be introduced together into raw meals during cement kiln co-processing hazardous wastes containing Cu, unfortunately the cooperation effects of fluorine and copper on the properties of cement clinker are still vague, it directly restricts the resource utilization of these wastes in the cement industry. Therefore, the cooperation effects of fluorine (CaF2) and copper (CuO) on the formation and properties of tricalcium silicate (C3S) were unveiled. The results indicated that a small cooperation addition of CuO could reduce distinctly f-CaO content of C3S doped with CaF2, and its burnability would be promoted notably, the immobilization of fluorine and copper in doped C3S also were promoted. Compared with C3S doped with CaF2, a cooperation addition of CuO and CaF2 further improved the formation of C3S grains and increased the structural symmetry of C3S crystal. The cooperation effects triggered the diffraction peaks for C3S polymorphisms to shift right, and induced the visible defects on the surface of C3S grains. In the current incorporation amounts of CaF2 and CuO into C3S, F- and Cu2+ would dissolve in its structure possibly by the replacement of O2– and Ca2+ respectively. CaF2 addition accelerated the initial hydration, but postponed the later hydration of C3S. The initial hydration was further accelerated by a cooperation addition of CuO, and its effects would be quite different if changing cooperation amounts of CaF2, accelerating or decelerating the hydration process of doped C3S relied on the cooperation amounts of CaF2 and CuO. The findings in this work would be expected to provide a promising solution to reduce the large energy consumption and CO2 emission in cement industry.
1_Introduction:
Nowadays, people constantly benefit from the visible convenience brought by the high-quality development of science and technology, concurrently they are also subject to the knotty burden of the enormous waste generation and the latent environmental contamination brought by the booming growth of the global population and the ever-intensifying industrialization. The World Bank data revealed that the global generation of wastes in 2016 was about 2.00 billion tons, it will probably crept up to 2.60 billion tons in 2030 and 3.40 billion tons in 2050 [1]. Take the example of China, the 3.28 billion tons of industrial solid waste, 173 million tons of municipal solid waste and 25 million tons of sludge were produced only in 2016 [2]. Roughly 77.00% of the solid wastes were presently still disposed in the open landfills or were transported to the waste burning facilities [3], in addition to the extensive occupation of valuable land resource, it would make a big threat to air, soil and water environment [4].
Cement has been recognized as the most widely applied artificial materials in the modern buildings, traffic infrastructures and marine constructions [5]. It is reported the cement production of China was 2.77 billion tons in 2018 with an increasing rate of 3.0% per year [6], and its production already surpassed more than half of the global cement production [7]. The tremendous demand of cement not only bring huge challenges, but also take good opportunities, the shortage of natural raw materials of cement production, the great energy consumption and the large CO2 emissions triggered a consideration of the utilization of solid waste as alternative raw materials in cement production [8]. The wastes from different industries containing calcium, silicon, aluminum and iron could be introduced as alternative raw materials into cement raw meals, till now cement kiln co-processing has been a very promising harmless treatment and resource reutilization for the industrial solid wastes [9], municipal solid waste [10], sludge [11], and even the hazardous wastes [12–15]. Nevertheless, some new problems gradually appeared during the co-processing process. Heavy metals and some impurity elements in these wastes might combine with cement clinker mineral phases during sintering at high temperature, theses impurities might alter the burnability, mineral compositions, and microstructure of produced clinker [16,17], then could affect the hydration characteristic and macro properties of produced cement [18,19], so the sufficient attention and discussion on the above problems is pivotal to implement waste utilization in cement kiln co-processing.
Copper (Cu) is a common hazardous element in the solid wastes, sludge and fossil fuels, e.g. copper slags [20], copper tailings [21], municipal solid waste [22], sewage sludge [23], and the polluted soil [24]. It has been realized that copper Cu would mainly be incorporated into the clinker minerals with cement kiln co-processing Cu-containing wastes, and it would influence on the hydration process and mechanical properties of the clinker [25]. Kakali et al. [26] revealed that CuO is beneficial to stimulate the combination of free CaO in the clinker at sintering temperature of 1000℃～1300℃, and reduced clinkering temperature by about 50℃. Ma et al. [13] reported that CuO increased the formation and growth of C3S, and R-type C3S would be transformed into M3 type. The addition of CuO more than 1.00% would prolong the induction period of hydration, accelerate the initial reaction rate and acceleration period. Some researchers discussed that the delayed effect of CuO on hydration process mainly due to formation of Cu(OH)2 [27] or Ca2(OH)4 ·4Cu(OH)2·2H2O [28], it might enter the covering layer of hydration products on the surface of clinker minerals and inhibit further hydration. Additionally, Shih et al. [29] and Chen et al. [30] pointed that Cu2+ in the wastes would be solidified in hydration products with trace amounts of leaching toxicity below the leaching limit when the CuO doped clinker hydrated.
Fluorine (F) is the widely applied mineralizer in cement kiln, and also is the major pollutants of the semiconductor-industry sludge [31], fluoride wastewater sludge [32], and the stainless-steel pickling sludge [33]. CaF2 could effectively reduce the clinkering temperature by 50℃～100℃, stimulate the formation of clinker minerals especially for alite, and lessen the large consumption of coal [34–35]. Yamashita et al. [36] discovered that the addition of CaF2 in clinker could decrease the viscosity and surface tension of the liquid melt state, the solid-state diffusion would be enhanced effectively. Tran et al. [37] and Boughanmi et al. [38] proposed that F- of CaF2 could be preferentially incorporated into C3S structure with the substitution of the O2− not linked to silicon, an excess of positive charge by F- substitute O2– would be compensated by the calcium vacancy, then it would change the hydration characteristic of the doped C3S by changing its polymorph symmetry and introducing the crystal defects [39]. Emanuelson et al. [40] and Moir et al. [41] realized that the doping amounts of F in clinker should be 0.25%～0.60% to obtain proper properties of clinker, once excessive fluoride was incorporated, the hydration process would be postponed and the properties would be weakened.
However, it is inevitable that fluorine from fluorite mineralizer and copper would be introduced into raw meals at the same time when the wastes containing copper were co-processed in current cement kiln. The introduced F and Cu will participate clinkering reactions in cement clinker preparation, however, it is still unknown that the effects of simultaneous existence of F and Cu on the formation and properties of cement clinker minerals, in addition, the related researches about the above concerns were rare so far. Tring to addressing and comprehending the collective influences of F and Cu on cement clinker is a key issue to promote the co-processing wastes containing copper in cement kiln.
Thereupon, a main mineral of Portland cement clinker of tricalcium silicate (C3S) was chose as the research object, CaF2 and CuO were used as the source of F and Cu to simulate the clinking process. The cooperation effects of F and Cu on the formation, C3S polymorphisms, microstructures, and hydration process of C3S would be explored by XRD, SEM-EDS, XPS and isothermal heat flow calorimetry. These findings in this work are expected to provide theoretical supports to the comprehensive utilization of hazardous Cu-containing wastes in cement kiln.
2_Materials and methods:
2.1 Materials  2.1.1 Raw materials The doped and undoped C3S samples were synthesized using a conventional solid-state sintering method [42]. The starting materials used are all analytical grade chemical reagents SiO2, CaCO3, CaF2, and CuO, and the starting material compositions of doped C3S samples were presented in Table 1 . The analytical grade CaCO3 and SiO2 were the starting materials for undoped C3S, the analytical grade CaF2 and CuO were dopants to prepare doped C3S, in addition, the doping amounts of CaF2 in C3S were 1.00%, 1.50% and 2.00%, the cooperation doping amounts of CuO in C3S were 0.25%, 0.50% and 1.00%. The previous study [43] already noted that the introduction of CaF2 would bring a spare calcium atom into the structure of C3S, which would break the original chemical form of C3S, thus the actual addition of CaCO3 should subtract the equivalent CaCO3 caused by addition of CaF2.   2.1.2 Preparation of experimental specimens Firstly, the analytical grade CaCO3 and SiO2 powders (the mole ratio CaO/SiO2 is 3:1) with/without CaF2 and CuO would be fully mixed with ethanol (solid liquid ratio is 1:10) in a magnetic stirrer for 24 h, and then the mixed paste was dried at 50℃ for 24 h. Secondly, these powders couple with 10.0% ethanol were pressed into cylindrical pellets (diameter is 50 mm and height is 20 mm) under 40.0 MPa. The prepared pellets with different compositions were calcined in tubular high temperature furnace XCSL-16–17 V at 1500℃, the calcination procedures were showed in Table 2  [43]. After every calcination cycle, free lime (f-CaO) contents of the calcined C3S samples were tested until it is less than 1.00%. If f-CaO content was beyond 1.00%, the air-quenched calcined samples would be reground to powders, pelletized and calcined again. The well-prepared calcined C3S samples would be selected to crack into small pieces for the measurements of SEM-EDS, and some other pieces would be ground into powders to pass through 75 μm sieve for the tests of burnability, immobilization ratios, XRD, XPS and heat flow.
2.2 Methods  2.2.1 Burnability and immobilization measurements The f-CaO content is a good indicator for the burnability of doped C3S samples, the less amounts would reveal good solid state reaction between C2S and CaO. The f-CaO content of C3S samples was measured by the ethanol-glycol method using F Ca-2008 free lime measuring instrument. The immobilization ratios of Cu and F element in the samples were measured according to the methods published by Yang et al. [44]. 3_Results and discussions:
3.1 Burnability and immobilization ratios To unveil the effects of fluorine and copper on burnability of doped C3S samples, the f-CaO contents were measured, and the results were depicted in Fig. 1 . It is indicated that the f-CaO content of undoped C3S was high as 0.9345%, yet, the addition of CaF2 could well better the burnability to reduce the f-CaO content, and the f-CaO content of the doped C3S with 2.00% CaF2 reached 0.1726%. The above results demonstrated the melting and mineralization effect of fluoride [36]. It is interesting to find that a trace of CuO was incorporated into CaF2 doped C3S could prominently decrease the f-CaO content for an excellent burnability. The results showed that the f-CaO content of the doped C3S with 1.00% CaF2 and 0.25% CuO reduced by 46.64% compared with 1.00% CaF2 doped C3S, and the f-CaO content of the doped C3S with 2.00% CaF2 and 1.00% CuO even reach 0.0054%. It could be found that the combined addition of CaF2 and CuO had the distinct cooperation effects on the burnability beyond single addition of CaF2 or CuO [13]. The immobilization of Cu and F in the doped C3S samples were described in Table 3 . The results showed that the immobilization ratios of Cu and F were all above 99% in these doped samples, and the more addition of CaF2 make more immobilization ratios of F. In addition, the incorporation of a few amounts of CuO into doped C3S with CaF2 could slightly stimulate the immobilization of F and Cu. Thus, incorporating CuO into C3S doped with CaF2 could simultaneously promote the immobilization of hazardous element F and Cu, and its promotion might result from the change of the liquid-state phase properties by the cooperation effects of CaF2 and CuO [18].
3.2 Mineral compositions of doped C3S and C3S polymorphisms It is recognized that the different C3S polymorphisms include triclinic (T1, T2 and T3), monoclinic (M1and M3) and rhombohedral (R) could be identified by the regional XRD patterns in the 2θ ranges of 31.5°～33° and 51°～52.5° [47,48], additionally, the hydration and mechanical properties of C3S with different polymorphism might be further improved or weakened [49,50]. Therefore, it is necessary to discuss the effects of CaF2 and CuO on the mineral compositions and polymorphisms revealed by XRD with various scanning parameters. Fig. 2  presented full XRD patterns of doped C3S samples, the built-in figures were characteristic diffraction positions of polymorphisms. Then Table 4  summarized the main mineral compositions and C3S polymorphisms of these doped samples. The results in Fig. 2 indicated that the main mineral composition in these samples were only alite without other minerals even in the doped samples with 2.00% CaF2 and 1.00% CuO after successive calcination under 1500℃. It implied that the addition of CaF2 and CuO into C3S would not alter the final mineral compositions. In the meantime, the diffraction intensity of alite came to be stronger with more addition of CaF2, it stated that the addition of CaF2 would benefit to promote the alite formation and improve its crystallizability [16]. It was found that the more addition of CuO into doped C3S with CaF2 could lead to the stronger diffraction of alite, its crystallizability might be further promoted by small amounts of CuO addition as well. It could be noticed in Fig. 2 that three diffraction peaks in the range of 31.5°～33°, and other three peaks in the range of 51°～52.5° of undoped C3S sample, it is a typical characteristics of triclinic T3 form with relatively low symmetric C3S crystal structure [42]. The structural symmetry of the doped C3S with 1.00% CaF2 increased as the polymorphism coexistence of T3 and monoclinic M1, and its main polymorphism was identified as M1 form [47]. A little addition of 0.25% CuO could also promote the structural symmetry even though the C3S presented the polymorphism coexistence of T3 and M1, the characteristic of M1 came to clearer. With the addition of CuO increasing to 0.50%, its structural symmetry became higher with monoclinic M3 form [49]. However, it was worth noting that the symmetry started to reduce from M3 to M1 with the addition of CuO increasing to 1.00%. The results in Table 4 indicated that the structural symmetry of doped C3S samples all would increase with CaF2 (≤2.00%) and CuO (＜1.00%) addition increasing, but its symmetry would be lowered as the addition of CuO was 1.00%. Ma et al. [13] once reported that the excessive addition of 3.00% CuO in doped clinker induced R C3S gradually transform into M3 with reduction of symmetry. Thus, the incorporation of CuO and CaF2 into C3S would accelerate the symmetry reduction only with 1.00% addition of CuO. The detail region diffraction positions of different doped samples were observed, and it was found that the characteristic diffraction peaks in the range of 31.5°～33° and 51°～52.5° had a tendency of shifting to larger diffraction angles, and its tendency was gradually more obvious as CaF2 and CuO addition increasing. According to the Bragg equation (  nÎ»=2d sin Î¸  ), with the increase of diffraction angle, the d value decreases and the cell volume decreases. In the above cases, the partial replacement of O2– (radius-140 pm) of C3S by F- (radius-136 pm) [37] and the partial substitution of Ca2+ (radius-99 pm) of C3S by Cu2+ (radius-76 pm) might result in the decrease of C3S cell structure [51].
3.3 Microstructure and element distributions of doped C3S The cooperation effects of fluorine and copper on the microstructure of doped C3S were revealed in Fig. 3 , Fig. 4  and Fig. 5 . Fig. 3 indicated that the internal structure of the undoped C3S was quite porous with small crystalline grains, its crystalline mainly grew together with each other, and it presented a slow growth trend from inside to outside due to the poor high temperature reaction environment, additionally, the surface of the crystals was smooth without defects, and the interface was clear. It could be conjectured that the formation of C3S was quietly difficult without the fluxing materials [16], and its formation would only depend on the solid state reaction between C2S and CaO. The results in Fig. 4 showed that the internal structure became compact after adding 2.00% CaF2, and the size of crystalline grains became big, however, its surface came to be rough with obvious defects that might be caused by the accelerated iterative growth of new crystals on primary crystals, the interface between crystals was also vague. It stated that the formation of C3S was accelerated with CaF2, but the crystal defects were increased. The microstructure of doped C3S with 2.00% CaF2 and 1.00% CuO in Fig. 5 showed that the formation of C3S was further promoted by the cooperation of CaF2 and CuO, its calcined structure was more compact, and the crystals continuously grew to be a big conjoined body, the defects on the crystals were easy to find as well. To explore the distribution characteristics of fluorine and copper in the doped C3S after calcination, EDS was used in this paper. Fig. 6  and Fig. 7  were element distribution maps of doped C3S with 2.00% CaF2 and doped C3S with 2.00% CaF2 and 1.00% CuO, respectively. Every element has a different color, and its brightness of that stands for the relatively contents of every element in selected areas. Fig. 6 showed that F element was more likely to be concentrated at the interface of C3S grains, and its distribution characteristic might relate with the changes of the hydration process of CaF2 doped C3S [38]. The distribution maps of F, Cu, O and Ca elements in Fig. 7 indicated that the distribution of F was more concentrated than that of Cu, the distribution of Cu was quite dispersed, and a few of Cu were also concentrated in the interface of C3S grains.
3.4 Binding forms of fluorine and copper in doped C3S To figure out the difference of the distribution characteristics between fluorine and copper in the doped C3S, and to understand the chemical valence states of fluorine and copper, the binding forms of fluorine and copper were analysed by XPS. The survey spectral and F spectral of doped C3S with 2.00% CaF2 were showed in Fig. 8  (a) and (b), the survey spectral, F spectral and Cu spectral of doped C3S with 2.00% CaF2 and 1.00% CuO were showed in Fig. 9  (a), (b) and (c). Fig. 8 revealed that fluorine only had a one Gaussian fitting peak F1s at binding energy of 684.6 eV in narrow spectrum, it was well corresponding to the F- in Ca-F bond [46], and any other minerals containing F could not be detected in the doped C3S by regional XRD rescanning, it means that addition of CaF2 less than 2.00% would not reach its incorporation solution limits into C3S [25]. Therefore, F- of CaF2 would likely enter C3S structure by the replacement of O2– of C3S to combine with Ca2+. The above findings would result in the defects of C3S crystal lattice, and thereupon the C3S characteristic diffraction peaks might come to shift right.  Fig. 9 demonstrated that a Gaussian fitting peak of fluorine was noticed at binding energy of 684.6 eV as F1s, which meant that the co-addition of Cu into C3S could not interfere the binding forms of F in doped C3S. Copper in doped C3S had two Cu 2p3/2 (933.1 eV) and Cu 2p1/2 (952.9 eV) main Gaussian fitting peaks with a visible satellite Gaussian fitting peak in the range of 940.0 eV～945.0 eV, it was corresponding to the Cu2+ of Cu–O bond [46], in addition, any other minerals containing F or Cu also could not be detected in the doped C3S by regional XRD rescanning, it also means that CaF2 and CuO would not reach their incorporation solution limits into C3S [25]. Therefore, F- would also likely enter the C3S structure, Cu2+ would possibly enter C3S structure by substituting Ca2+ due to its similar electrochemical properties between Cu2+ and Ca2+ [18,52]. The above results could verify the distinct right shifting of C3S characteristic diffraction peaks.
3.5 Hydration heat evolution of doped C3S The cooperation effects of fluorine and copper on the hydration characteristics of doped C3S were revealed by hydration heat evolution in Fig. 10 , Fig. 11  and Fig. 12 . The hydration heat evolution of doped C3S in Fig. 10 showed that a rapid exothermic peak arrived in the initial period within 10 min, it mainly rely on the dissolution rate of alite [53]. The addition of CaF2 accelerated the initial hydration rate, and heat flow of doped C3S with 1.00% CaF2 could reach 0.115 W/g, while it was 0.091 W/g of undoped C3S. The accelerated initial hydration might origin from the increase hydration active points caused by the change of microstructure and defects on the surface of alite [54]. In the next induction period, it could be found that CaF2 prolonged the induction period, and its duration reached 7.78 h, 7.80 h and even 38.3 h with the addition of CaF2 increasing, besides, the highest heat flow in the acceleration period was reduced markedly due to addition of CaF2. Hence, CaF2 addition could prolong the induction period, postpone the acceleration period, and decrease the later hydration rates of doped C3S. The results in Fig. 10 (b) showed that the cumulative heat release of C3S in the induction period was increased by CaF2 addition, and then the cumulative heat release would be always lower than that of undoped C3S. As for the changes of hydration process of C3S caused by CaF2 addition might result from the accelerated initial hydration due to the changed microstructure and increased defects [55], and began to form a relatively dense layer of the initial hydration products on the surface of unhydrated C3S, and then distinctly hinder the further hydration of doped C3S [39], besides, the characteristics of the initial hydration products containing F of CaF2 doped C3S may differ from that of the undoped C3S, and it would also interfere the subsequent hydration reaction of doped C3S [56]. The hydration heat evolution of doped C3S with 1.00% CaF2 and different amounts of CuO in Fig. 11 demonstrated that an obvious exothermic peak existed after contacting water in about 10 min, and the initial hydration rates were quite higher than that of doped with 1.00% CaF2. With the addition of CuO increasing, it would gradually increase as 0.165 W/g, 0.166 W/g and 0.186 W/g. The addition of CuO into doped C3S with CaF2 directly promoted the initial hydration rate possibly due to its increased surface defects and the change of microstructures [57]. The duration of induction period shortened with the addition of CuO with different degrees, and in the acceleration period, its hydration heat flow was much higher than the doped C3S without CuO. The results in Fig. 11 (b) indicated that the cumulative heat release of doped C3S with 1.00% CaF2 and different amounts of CuO in the induction period were quite higher than that of doped C3S with 1.00% CaF2, in the next periods, the cumulative heat release of doped C3S would always be higher than that of doped C3S with 1.00% CaF2. Therefore, it could be noted that the small incorporation of CuO into CaF2 doped C3S presented the apparent cooperation effects on the hydration process, the addition of CuO accompanied with CaF2 shortened the induction period, advanced the acceleration period, and increased its hydration rates. The hydration heat evolution of doped C3S with 2.00% CaF2 and CuO in Fig. 12 testified that the initial hydration could be promoted by the addition of 2.00% CaF2 and CuO, and its heat flow reached 0.182 W/g, 0.174 W/g, and 0.174 W/g with the addition of CuO increasing. Even though the duration of the induction period came to lessen as 16.98 h, 23.05 h and 57.80 h compared with that of doped C3S with 2.00% CaF2, the hydration heat flow was seriously hindered when the addition of CuO was more than 0.50%, while the addition of CuO below 0.25% would shorten the induction period, advance the acceleration period, and increase its hydration rates. The addition of CuO beyond 0.50% sharply reduced the hydration heat flow of the doped C3S. Tao et al. [58] once discussed the retardation mechanisms caused by CuO that Cu2+ might be more competitive than Ca2+ of the doped C3S for nucleophilic attacks during the hydration process, it was due to the relatively lower Cu3d orbitals to obtain electrons easily from anions OH– released by H2O, and the prior hydroxylation of Cu2+ will reduce the concentration of OH– in the hydrated solution to further delay the oversaturation of portlandite and the other hydration products. Additionally, the changed characteristics of the initial hydration products containing F and Cu might change the later hydration process of the doped C3S [13]. However, it might need more confirmations by intuitive methods to explain the complicated hydration mechanisms of doped C3S with CaF2 and CuO.
4_Conclusions:
In this work, the cooperation effects of fluorine and copper on the formation and properties of prepared C3S were revealed by XRD, SEM-EDS, XPS and isothermal heat flow calorimetry. The following findings could be obtained.
Although CaF2 reduced f-CaO content of C3S and improved its burnability, a small cooperation addition of CuO only as 0.25% could reduce distinctly f-CaO content of C3S, and its burnability was substantially promoted. The cooperation effects of CaF2 and CuO strengthened the immobilization of fluorine and copper in doped C3S matrix.
The cooperation addition of CaF2 and CuO into C3S enhanced the formation and growth of alite grains, and ensured C3S polymorphisms with higher structural symmetry keep stable at room temperature. The characteristic diffraction peaks of C3S shifted to the larger angles with the co-addition of CaF2 and CuO. The cooperation addition made many defects on the surface of C3S grains visible. Within current incorporation amounts, F- and Cu2+ would dissolve in C3S structure possibly by the replacement of O2– and Ca2+ respectively.
CaF2 addition accelerated the initial hydration, prolonged the induction period, postponed the acceleration period, and decelerated the later hydration of C3S. The initial hydration of C3S was further accelerated by cooperation addition of CuO, and its effects were quite different if changing cooperation amounts of CaF2, at that time, accelerating or decelerating the hydration process of doped C3S would depend on the cooperation amounts of CaF2 and CuO.
We realized the mechanisms about the huge changes of hydration characteristics of doped C3S with F and Cu remain to be confirmed by other measurements, but the current findings in this work might be the valuable foundation to promote the value-added utilization of these hazardous wastes containing Cu in cement kiln. Based on that, we try to apply this cooperation effects to provide a solution on reducing the large CO2 emissions of cement industry.
