Title: Synergistic effects of CuO and CaF2 additives in facilitating low-temperature tricalcium silicate formation and stabilization
Abstract: This study investigates the effects of CuO, CaF₂, and their combination on phase formation in C₃S (alite) clinkers at different firing temperatures, aiming to reduce energy consumption in clinker production. Clinker samples with 0.1 wt.% CuO, 0.8 wt.% CaF₂, and a combination of 0.1 wt.% CuO and 0.8 wt.% CaF₂ were synthesized and fired at temperatures between 1200 °C and 1350 °C. The mineralogical composition of the clinkers was analyzed using X-ray diffraction patterns with Rietveld refinement technique. The results showed that alite formation was absent below 1350 °C in clinkers without additives. The addition of CuO promoted belite (C₂S) formation and reduced free lime content but did not significantly induce alite formation. In contrast, CaF₂ significantly enhanced alite formation, yielding monoclinic M                     1 and M                     3 polymorphs, with M                     1 being the dominant phase. The addition of 0.8 wt.% CaF₂ accelerated alite phase content of 18.96 wt.% at 1200 °C, which further increased to 73.54 wt.% at 1350 °C. The combined addition of CuO and CaF₂ further improved alite formation at lower temperatures, with alite content higher than 50 wt.% at 1250 °C. These findings demonstrate that CuO and CaF₂ act synergistically to facilitate alite formation at reduced firing temperatures, providing a potential pathway for energy-efficient clinker production.
1_Introduction:
Demand for cement is on the rise worldwide as a result of infrastructure development and modernization efforts. In 2020, the estimated global production of cement reached 4.1 billion tonnes [1]. Moreover, the World Cement Association (WAC) estimated global cement production is expected to reach 8.2 billion tonnes by 2030 [2]. At the same time, the global cement sector stands as a significant source of carbon dioxide emissions, accounting for >7 % of total global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions [3,4]. During cement manufacturing, most CO2 emissions stem from the decomposition of limestone, the primary component of cement, and the combustion required to maintain temperatures around 1500 °C. Reports indicate that for every ton of cement produced, between 0.73 and 0.85 tons of CO2 are emitted [5]. An interesting approach to improve the cement manufacturing process involves finding strategies to lower the calcination temperature, thereby reducing both energy use and CO2 emissions. Typically, kilns used for this process operate at temperatures between 1400 and 1500 °C [6]. Energy expenses make up about 30–50 percent of the total production costs in cement manufacturing. Additionally, the production of each ton of cement consumes approximately 100–110 kWh of electricity [7]. The burning of fuels in kilns is responsible for roughly 30 % of the total CO2 emissions from the production processes [8,9].
Several previous studies conducted in various laboratories have explored how mineralizers can lower the temperature required for clinker burning [10–13]. These studies have observed that incorporating small amounts of these inorganic substances can significantly reduce energy consumption. Mineralizers have also been found to potentially enhance the hydraulic properties of Portland clinker in certain situations [14,15]. Extensive research has focused on the impact of mineralizers in the formation of clinker minerals and the phase changes that occur during clinkerization [16–18].
The CaO-SiO₂ system has been extensively studied in several investigations [19–21]. In Portland cement, C₃S and C₂S are the primary hydraulic phases, undergoing multiple phase transformations. The complex solid solutions of C₃S and C₂S are referred to as “alite” and “belite”, respectively. C₂S undergoes several phase transformations over a range of temperatures (Fig. 1 (a)). Different C₂S modifications can be stabilized at room temperature through doping with certain ions [22]. C₃S is formed above 1250 °C through the reaction of C₂S and CaO. The phase transformations of C₃S are summarized in Fig. 1(b).
Researchers have extensively studied calcium fluoride (CaF2) for its role in the clinkerization process of cement production, where it acts as a mineralizer to enhance the efficiency of the process. Da et al. [24] indicated that CaF2 can significantly reduce the clinkerization temperature by 50 °C to 100 °C, which is a critical factor in energy consumption and carbon emissions in cement manufacturing. Yamashita et al. [25] found that incorporating CaF2 into clinker reduces both the viscosity and surface tension of the melt in its liquid state, effectively enhancing solid-state diffusion. The crystal structure is influenced by defect reactions that occur when fluoride anions were incorporated into the C3S structure. The pure C3S typically exhibits the triclinic form (T), the lowest symmetry. However, doping C3S with 1.0 wt% CaF2 results in a transition to the monoclinic form (M). Further, when the doping is increased to 2.0 wt% CaF2, the C3S polymorph changes into the rhombohedral form (R) [26]. Emanuelson et al. [27] highlighted that the enhancement in the hydraulic activity of mineralized clinker is primarily due to defect introductions from substitutions, rather than changes in the polymorph symmetry of alite. They explained that the reduced hydraulic activity in mineralized clinker could be linked to high fluoride content, specifically in case of fluorine content higher than 0.4 wt%. This might be due to the formation of insoluble layers on the clinker mineral surfaces that act as barriers. Thus, to achieve optimal performance in the resulting clinkers, the fluoride content should be kept between approximately 0.5–1.2 % by weight [27–29].
CuO has been found to enhance the combination of free CaO in the clinker, particularly within the temperature range of 1000 °C to 1300 °C, and it has the effect of reducing the clinkering temperature by a minimum of 50 °C [30]. When CuO is incorporated into clinker, it facilitates the accelerated formation and growth of C3S, and induces the transformation of C3S from rhombohedral (R) to monoclinic (M 3) form. These effects can be attributed to the influence of CuO on the characteristics of the liquid phase, including the temperature at which it forms, its quantity, and its viscosity [16].
As previously mentioned, it is clear that the addition of either CaF2 or CuO contributes to lowering the firing temperature and influences the phase formation and crystal structure of clinker. For this reason, some researchers have attempted to explore the co-doping effects of fluorine and copper on clinker formation [24,31,32]. Tiantong et al. [31] conducted research on the impact of incorporating 0.8 wt.% CaF2 and 0.1 wt.% CuO while adjusting the firing temperatures between 1100 °C and 1325 °C in the production of alite calcium sulfoaluminate clinkers. Their findings indicated that the addition of CaF2 and CuO significantly aided phase development, particularly by facilitating the formation of C3S at lower temperatures. With these additives, clinkers were initially forming C3S at a firing temperature of 1100 °C, whereas clinkers lacking these additives required a minimum temperature of 1325 °C. The synergistic effects of fluorine (CaF2) and copper (CuO) on the formation and properties of tricalcium silicate (C3S) were studied by Da et al. [24]. The study varied the doping levels of CaF2 in C3S at 1.00 %, 1.50 %, and 2.00 %, while the cooperative doping levels of CuO were set at 0.25 %, 0.50 %, and 1.00 %, using a firing temperature of 1500 °C. The findings revealed that even minor additions of CuO significantly reduced the free CaO content in CaF2-doped C3S, enhancing its sinterability. The co-doping also improved the formation of C3S grains and increased the structural symmetry of the C3S crystal.
Although previous studies have demonstrated the effects of CuO and CaF2 co-doping on clinker formation, their scope was often limited to altering doping levels without varying firing temperatures. Conversely, other investigations have explored the impact of these dopants on the formation of C3S by adjusting firing temperatures, while maintaining constant doping levels. The current research extensively investigates how different co-doping levels of CuO and CaF2 affect the phase formation of tricalcium silicate polymorphisms across a range of firing temperatures. The results of this study should deepen understanding of the synergistic effects of fluorine and copper on the synthesis of cement clinker under various firing temperatures, thereby offering insights into optimizing clinker production processes.
2_Materials and methods:
2.1 Sample preparation High-purity chemical reagents, CaCO3 and SiO2, were used as raw materials for synthesizing C3S to eliminate the effects of impurity ions such as K+, Mg2+, and Cl- found in industrial raw materials. The oxide ratio by mass of SiO2 to CaO was fixed at 0.357 according to Taylor [33]. CaF2 and/or CuO were added to the raw mixes in various amounts. Table 1  provides the detailed compositions of the different C3S samples doped with CaF2 and CuO additives. It should be noted that the excess calcium from the introduction of CaF2 into the doped C3S samples was not considered. To minimize the influence of particle size distribution on phase formation at high temperatures, the particle size distribution of all starting materials was analyzed, as shown in Fig. 2 . All raw materials and additives exhibited a favorable particle size distribution with a similar mean diameter. After weighing the raw materials according to their designed content, they were mixed and milled using zirconia balls for 24 h in ethanol. The wet slurry was dried on a hot plate, then ground and sieved through a 75 µm sieve. Particles that did not pass through the sieve were reground and re-sieved until they met the size requirement. The samples were mixed with a small amount of ethanol to make molding easier and then molded into spherical shapes with a diameter of 1 cm to promote good contact between solid phases during the sintering process [34]. The clinkerization temperature range of 1200 °C to 1350 °C was selected based on the effect of fluoride addition, which lowers the minimum alite formation temperature from 1350 °C to approximately 1050 °C [35]. The maximum temperature was set at 1350 °C, as belite and free CaO react to form alite in the presence of a liquid phase above 1300 °C. To balance experimental feasibility and process optimization, a 50 °C increment was chosen, aligning with previous studies that explored temperature variations for optimizing clinker formation while minimizing CO₂ emissions and energy consumption [36]. The molded samples were calcined at 900 °C for 30 min at a heating rate of 5 °C per minute to decompose CaCO3 to CaO and CO2 [31]. After the decomposition period, the clinkerization temperature was increased to one of four different maximum temperatures (1200 °C, 1250 °C, 1300 °C, or 1350 °C) for 30 min. Finally, the samples were quickly quenched from the high temperature using airflow to stabilize the hydraulic phases.
2.2 Characterization of clinkers The mineralogical composition of the clinkers was investigated using the XRD analytical technique. The XRD patterns were measured on a Bruker-D8 ENDEAVOR Diffractometer (CuKα, λ = 0.15406 nm) operated at 45 kV and 30 mA at room temperature. The detection range was between 8°–65° with a step size of 0.02°. The Rietveld refinement quantitative phase analysis was conducted to obtain the quantitative phase content in clinker using DIFFRAC.SUITE TOPAS V.5.0 software. The observed diffraction patterns were refined by fitting the simulated patterns to determine the crystal structures and the modal amounts of minerals. The inorganic crystal structure database (ICSD) codes for all identified phases in the studied clinkers via the Rietveld refinement technique are also given in Table 2 . Generally, the weighted profile residual (R wp) and the goodness of fit (GOF) are normally used to assess the quality of the fits in the Rietveld refinement processes. The refined result would be considered reliable if the R wp was <12 % and the GOF lower than 4 [31]. These criteria were set for the refinement processes in this study. Before XRD analysis, clinkers were finely ground using a disc mill at a ratio of 1100 rpm for 1 min and sieved through a 75 µm sieve, with the passing fraction used for testing. The morphology and microstructure of clinkers fired at 1350 °C were also investigated via a scanning electron microscope (SEM) model Leo1455VP. The elemental composition of the selected clinker phases was determined using energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) by average from three points.
3_Results and discussion:
3.1 Effect of CuO and CaF2 single additive on clinkerization  Fig. 3  shows the XRD patterns of clinker prepared at different firing temperatures for the three test groups: the reference (Fig. 3(a)), clinker with 0.1 wt.% CuO (Fig. 3(b)), and clinker with 0.8 wt.% CaF2 (Fig. 3(c)). Comparing the intensity of XRD peaks, the reference clinker (without additives) fired at 1200 °C exhibited primarily free lime and belite as the main phases. Even when the firing temperature increased to 1350 °C, the XRD pattern showed only slight changes, indicating that the phase composition remained relatively stable at higher temperatures. In the clinker with 0.1 wt.% CuO, belite and free lime were still the predominant phases, although the diffraction peaks of belite were more pronounced than those of free lime (as shown in Zoom-in on Fig. 3). This suggests that the addition of CuO might have a subtle effect on the relative intensities of these phases but did not significantly alter the overall phase composition. In contrast, the clinker with 0.8 wt.% CaF2 showed the appearance of alite diffraction peaks. As the firing temperature increased, the intensity of alite peaks became more pronounced, while the intensity of the belite and free lime peaks decreased. This suggests that the addition of CaF2 facilitated the formation of alite, especially at higher temperatures, and influenced the phase transitions within the clinker. To enhance understanding and visualization of the effect of temperature on phase transformation in the clinker, the variation in phase composition of the clinkers fired at different temperatures shown plotted in Fig. 4 . In the reference clinkers, free lime and belite were the predominant crystalline phases, with only a limited presence of alite. The slight presence of the alite phase, approximately 6.31 wt.%, in the sample fired at 1250 °C can be attributed to the formation of a liquid phase, which facilitates the formation and development of alite crystals at this temperature [30]. The free lime content was approximately 50 wt.%, and it showed minimal variation with increasing firing temperature, maintaining relative stability up to 1350 °C. This stability in free lime levels suggests that phase transitions were restricted, as free lime did not convert significantly into belite or alite, even under elevated thermal conditions. The belite phases, primarily composed of β-C2S along with minor traces of α-C2S and γ-C2S polymorphs, began to form at 1200 °C. However, in the absence of a fluxing agent, belite showed limited interaction with free lime, preventing the effective formation of alite at temperatures below 1350 °C. This indicates that, without flux agents, the transformation pathway from belite and free lime to alite is significantly constrained, even at higher firing temperatures. In the 0.1CuO clinker, the free lime content showed a noticeable reduction compared to the reference clinker. Initially measured at approximately 31.93 wt.% at 1200 °C, an increase in firing temperature to 1250 °C caused the free lime content to slightly increase to 34.27 wt.%. Thereafter, further increases in firing temperature resulted in slight variations in free lime content, stabilizing at around 34.67 wt.% at 1350 °C. The lowest free lime content was obtained from the sample fired at a lower temperature, indicating the highest combined content of C₃S and C₂S phases. This suggests that CuO more effectively improves clinkerization at lower temperatures, consistent with a previous investigation [42], which found that CuO acts as both a mineralizer and a flux. CuO has been shown to be a more effective mineralizer at lower temperatures (1200 °C) compared to higher firing temperatures. In contrast, the reference clinker maintained a significantly higher free lime content, close to 50 wt.% across the temperature range up to 1350 °C. This suggests that the addition of 0.1 wt.% CuO in the clinker composition enhanced the reactivity of free lime, promoting its partial incorporation into the silicate phases even at lower temperatures. The lowering of the belite formation temperature by adding CuO may be attributed to the dissolution of CuO in the raw materials, which decreases the formation temperature of the liquid phase and increases the amount of liquid phase [16]. Moreover, the addition of CuO influenced the relative proportions of γ-C2S and β-C2S as the temperature changed, leading to notable transformations in phase composition. The β-C2S was the dominant phase at 1200 °C, accounting for 56.76 wt.%, while γ-C2S was present at a relatively low level of 5.13 wt.%. As the temperature increased to 1250 °C, there was a significant shift in the distribution between the two polymorphs, with γ-C2S content rising sharply to 25.19 wt.% and β-C2S decreasing to 38.56 wt.%. This trend continued as temperatures increased further, with γ-C2S content remaining substantial at 27.3 wt.% and 25.59 wt.% at 1300 °C and 1350 °C, respectively, while β-C2S content stabilized around 36–38 wt.%. The significant finding is that although adding CuO accelerates the formation of C2S phases at lower firing temperatures compared to samples without CuO, the coexistence of γ-C2S and β-C2S polymorphs is observed. It should be noted that β-C2S is a reactive phase, whereas γ-C2S lacks hydraulic properties [43]. Therefore, adding only CuO to enhance the clinkerization of alite or belite may not be an optimal approach. In the 0.8CaF₂ clinkers, the addition of CaF2 led to notable changes in phase composition, particularly with the formation of alite. The enhanced burnability of clinker and the facilitation of alite phase formation at low firing temperatures with fluoride addition can be attributed to both the reduced viscosity and surface tension of the oxide melt and the increased melt volume resulting from the eutectic formation of fluoride, which permits alite formation at lower temperatures [24,25]. 3.2 Effect of CuO-CaF2 dual additives doped on clinkerization The assessment of the effects of CuO and CaF2 as individual additives and the analysis of phase formation characteristics at various firing temperatures, the next phase of investigation involves examining the influence of co-adding both CuO and CaF2 on clinker phase development. The initial formulation incorporates 0.1 wt.% CuO and 0.8 wt.% CaF2, referred to as 0.1CuO0.8CaF2. Subsequently, the proportions are adjusted by increasing the CuO content while reducing the CaF2 content, resulting in the compositions 0.3CuO0.6CaF₂ and 0.5CuO0.4CaF₂. This approach yields a total of three formulations, each with systematically varied CuO and CaF2 ratios to evaluate their combined effects on phase transformation and stability. XRD patterns for clinkers produced at various firing temperatures are presented in Fig. 8 . The primary phases identified in all clinkers include alite, belite, free lime, and portlandite. Although the XRD patterns of clinkers with varying CuO and CaF2 contents do not exhibit any significant differences, the quantitative phase analysis conducted through the Rietveld refinement technique reveals some noteworthy findings, as listed in Tables 6–8   . The co-addition of CuO and CaF2 exerts a significant influence on the distribution and stability of belite polymorphs, particularly β-C2S and γ-C2S. In samples with CuO as the sole additive, a coexistence of γ-C2S and β-C2S polymorphs is observed (Table 4). Conversely, in co-doped samples, γ-C2S content decreases markedly, resulting in the exclusive presence of β-C2S across all CuO- CaF2 additive ratios. This observation suggests that the synergistic effect of CaF2 in conjunction with CuO enhances the stabilization of β-C2S, which positively impacts the development of cement strength relative to samples with CuO alone. An intriguing finding from the analysis of co-adding CuO and CaF2 to clinker polymorphs is observed in the alite crystals, as illustrated in Fig. 9 . Previous investigation demonstrated that adding CaF2 and CuO greatly influenced alite formation [31]. However, previous study has not examined the effects of varying the proportions of CuO and CaF2 on the crystal structure of alite, which is investigated in this investigation. It is evident that the addition of CuO and CaF2 promotes alite formation at a firing temperature of 1200 °C. Increasing the CuO proportion to 0.5 wt.% yields up to 36 wt.% alite at this relatively low firing temperature of 1200 °C. However, with increased firing temperatures, the alite phase content rises rapidly across all clinkers containing various proportions of CuO and CaF2. In compositions where CuO is entirely absent (0.8CaF₂) or present at a low level in co-addition with CaF2 (0.1CuO0.8CaF₂ clinkers), alite forms as both M 1 and M 3 polymorphs, with M 1 alite predominating over M 3 alite. As the CuO fraction increases, M 3 alite content also increases, ultimately higher than that of M 1 alite in proportion when CuO is raised to 0.5 wt.%. These findings provide essential insights and emphasize the need for cement researchers to carefully consider both the type and number of additives when optimizing alite phase composition. 4_Conclusions: This study investigated the effects of adding CuO, CaF₂, and a combination of CuOCaF₂ with varying firing temperatures during the production of C₃S clinkers. Findings revealed the following:  • In the absence of any additives, alite formation remained minimal even at a clinkerization temperature of 1350 °C. This indicates that the synthesis of C₃S using only raw materials, without the addition of CaF₂ or CuO as mineralizers, is ineffective in reducing the clinkerization temperature required for alite formation.   • The incorporation of CuO affected the phase composition, resulting in a reduction of free lime and an enhancement of belite concentration relative to the reference clinker. Nonetheless, despite these modifications, alite production remained minimal, indicating that CuO alone does not adequately enhance alite stability or crystallization at reduced firing temperatures.   • The addition of CaF₂ markedly improved alite production compared to the reference and CuO-containing clinkers. The generated alite crystals comprised both M 1 and M 3 alite polymorphs, with M 1 being the dominant variant. Adding 0.8 wt.% CaF₂ enhanced alite formation to 18.96 wt.% at 1200 °C, increasing significantly to 73.54 wt.% at 1350 °C, indicating that CaF₂ independently facilitates alite formation and phase transformation at lower temperatures.   • The simultaneous addition of CuO and CaF₂ induced alite formation at lower temperatures, similar to the effects observed with CaF₂ alone. However, adding CuO content in co-doped formulations notably enhanced M 3 alite polymorphs. The combination of 0.1 wt.% CuO and 0.8 wt.% CaF₂ increased alite content to higher than 50 wt.% at 1250 °C, significantly lower than the typical clinkerization temperature of 1450 °C for OPC synthesis. This suggests a synergistic effect between CuO and CaF₂, improving alite formation efficiency while influencing the stability of specific alite polymorphs.
